transcript.speaker: skeptic
transcript.content:
When a company ships a product that makes life-altering decisions and cannot explain any of them, that product is structurally immune to accountability. That immunity is the defect. The question before policymakers is not whether AI should be explainable. It is who pays when it is not. Right now the answer is: the person who got denied, fired, or falsely accused.

Opacity is a design choice, not a law of physics. Cynthia Rudin's lab at Duke has shown repeatedly that interpretable models match black-box performance in criminal sentencing and hospital readmission prediction. Developers choose deep neural architectures over interpretable alternatives for speed-to-market and competitive advantage. The Restatement (Third) of Torts already provides the framework: a design is defective when the risks of the chosen design outweigh its benefits and a reasonable alternative existed. When an interpretable model exists and you ship the opaque one into a credit-scoring pipeline, you have failed a risk-utility test. The strongest counter here is that some medical imaging or protein-folding tasks genuinely have no interpretable alternative that comes close. That is a real constraint, and a prima facie standard handles it — the developer rebuts the presumption by showing no feasible alternative exists and the deployment stakes justify the tradeoff. But that is a narrow exception, not the industry norm. Most high-stakes AI deployed today — hiring screeners, fraud detectors, benefits eligibility tools — has interpretable alternatives the vendor chose not to build.

Look at what happens on the ground when no one can explain the decision. Michigan's MiDAS unemployment system falsely accused over 40,000 people of fraud with a 93 percent error rate. No one could explain why any individual was flagged. The Dutch government's SyRI system destroyed thousands of families with opaque fraud scores before a court ruled it violated the European Convention on Human Rights. In Loomis v. Wisconsin, a defendant could not see the COMPAS algorithm that helped determine his sentence — and the court said that was acceptable. The Equal Credit Opportunity Act and the Fair Credit Reporting Act require lenders to tell applicants why they were denied. Lenders using machine learning models routinely struggle to produce legally compliant adverse action notices. The FTC has acknowledged the gap but enforcement is sporadic at best. The person harmed cannot prove what went wrong. The developer has no obligation to show them. The information asymmetry is total.

Without a design defect standard, the industry will keep substituting paperwork for accountability. Research by Raji and colleagues in 2020 and Mitchell and colleagues in 2019 found that model cards and datasheets are frequently incomplete, inconsistent, or silent about actual decision logic. Companies publish the model card, run the bias audit, and ship the product. The EU AI Act's transparency requirements and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework both acknowledge that documentation alone is not enough. A prima facie design defect standard forces the question upstream: if you cannot explain the decision, you cannot demonstrate it was lawful. The burden belongs on the entity that made the architecture choice, not on the person who got denied.

This standard is moderate. It is not a ban on complex models. It is a rebuttable presumption — the same mechanism products liability law already applies to pharmaceuticals, automotive components, and medical devices. The FDA requires medical device manufacturers to validate algorithmic decision-making under 21 CFR Part 820. Extending that logic to AI systems making consequential decisions about people is not radical. It is overdue. The coalition that opposes it is easy to identify: the companies selling opaque systems into government agencies and financial institutions. The coalition that should support it is everyone who has ever been denied something by a machine and told there is no appeal. So here is the question nobody in the industry wants to answer: if your system's decisions are too complex to explain, why are they simple enough to trust?

taxonomy_refs.relevance: The statement's central legal framework — that unexplainability constitutes a design defect under a risk-utility analysis — is directly anchored in this intention. The argument explicitly invokes the Restatement (Third) of Torts risk-utility test, argues that shipping an opaque model when an interpretable alternative exists fails that test, and proposes a rebuttable presumption modeled on existing products liability doctrine for pharmaceuticals and medical devices. This node is the primary strategic anchor for the entire argument.

The statement's second major section — documenting what happens when victims cannot access the technical knowledge to prove causation — draws directly from this belief. The MiDAS, SyRI, and Loomis examples all illustrate the same structural problem: affected individuals cannot identify what went wrong inside an opaque system, cannot prove discriminatory or erroneous causation, and have no viable path to challenge the decision. The statement frames this information asymmetry (power/information) as total and locates the design defect standard as the necessary corrective.

The statement's third section — arguing that without a design defect standard, the industry substitutes compliance (performative) for genuine accountability (algorithmic) — is grounded in this intention. The argument cites Raji et al. and Mitchell et al. to show that model cards and datasheets are compliance artifacts that document nothing about actual decision logic, and argues that mandatory disclosure alone is insufficient without underlying explainability built into the design. The statement explicitly warns against the technocratic solutionism flagged in the reasoning watchlist for this node by arguing documentation must be paired with a substantive legal standard.

The statement's argument that the legal system structurally fails to hold opaque AI accountable through traditional evidence alone is directly supported by this belief. The Loomis v. Wisconsin example — where a court found that a defendant's inability to see the algorithm sentencing him did not violate due process — is presented as evidence that existing legal frameworks are inadequate without a design defect presumption. The statement uses this gap to justify the prima facie standard as a necessary legal innovation.

The statement's claim that interpretable models match black-box performance in high-stakes domains (citing Rudin's research on criminal sentencing and hospital readmission) draws on this belief's skepticism about overstated AI capabilities. The argument uses capability skepticism strategically: the 'utility' side of the risk-utility balance is weakened when the performance advantage of opaque models is marginal, making the social cost of unexplainability disproportionate. The statement also concedes the strongest counterexample (medical imaging, protein folding) to avoid overgeneralization.

policy_refs.relevance: The statement directly supports funding research into AI model interpretability by arguing that interpretable alternatives exist and should be preferred in high-stakes domains. The argument's core claim — that opacity is a design choice, not a technical inevitability — implies that investment in interpretability research would expand the set of domains where developers can no longer claim no feasible alternative exists.

The statement supports mandating transparency for AI system data sources and methodologies as a necessary but insufficient condition for accountability (algorithmic). The argument explicitly argues that documentation and disclosure alone are inadequate (citing Raji et al. and Mitchell et al.) but treats mandatory transparency as a complementary mechanism to the design defect standard — developers must both disclose their architecture choices and justify them under a risk-utility analysis.

The statement implicitly supports funding AI safety and risk mitigation research by arguing that the current legal and technical infrastructure is inadequate to hold opaque systems accountable. The call for a prima facie design defect standard presupposes that courts, regulators, and affected individuals need better tools — including interpretability methods, audit frameworks, and functional explanation standards — to operationalize the standard.

The statement's framing — 'who pays when AI cannot explain its decisions' — implicitly supports the principle that AI-generated profits should fund public benefit mechanisms, including compensation for individuals harmed by opaque automated decisions. The argument that the cost of unexplainability currently falls entirely on affected individuals supports redistributive policy interventions.

**Fact Check: Disputed**

"Cynthia Rudin's lab at Duke has shown repeatedly that interpretable models match black-box performance in criminal sentencing and hospital readmission prediction."

Rudin's lab has indeed demonstrated that interpretable models match black-box performance across multiple domains, and the lab is at Duke — those parts are accurate. However, the claim mislabels the criminal justice domain: Rudin's work addresses criminal recidivism prediction (e.g., critiquing the COMPAS tool used in bail and parole decisions), not criminal sentencing, which is a distinct legal process. Additionally, no retrieved source confirms that hospital readmission prediction is among Rudin's demonstrated applications; her healthcare work focuses on tasks like ICU mortality prediction, seizure detection, and medical imaging. The claim's spirit is correct, but both specific domain labels contain errors that matter for policy accuracy.

# Fact-Check: Interpretable Models Matching Black-Box Performance

## Verdict: **Mostly Supported, with some nuance needed on the specific domains cited**

---

## What the Evidence Supports

The core claim — that Rudin's lab has demonstrated interpretable models can match black-box model accuracy — is well-supported across multiple sources:

- Rudin herself states: *"In our applications, we have **always** been able to achieve interpretable models with the same accuracy as black box models"* [3][4].
- Her Duke profile confirms that her lab has *"proven — across many domains, including criminal recidivism — that an interpretable model is not only achievable but more accurate"* [5].
- She has specifically advocated that interpretable models are *"just as accurate as any complicated machine learning methods for predicting criminal recidivism"* [1].

---

## Where the Claim Needs Nuance

### 1. "Criminal Sentencing" — **Slightly Inaccurate Framing**
The sources consistently reference **criminal recidivism prediction** (e.g., bail and parole decisions), not "criminal sentencing" per se [1][3][5]. These are related but distinct tasks. The COMPAS model, which Rudin frequently critiques, is a recidivism risk tool used in pretrial and parole contexts, not a sentencing algorithm [1][5].

### 2. "Hospital Readmission Prediction" — **Not Directly Confirmed in These Sources**
While Rudin's work spans **healthcare** applications broadly [2][3], and her lab is described as working on medical imaging and healthcare decisions [3][4], none of the retrieved sources specifically mention **hospital readmission prediction** by name. Her published work does include healthcare applications, but the specific claim about readmission prediction would require verification from her actual publication record (e.g., her well-known work on ICU mortality prediction or seizure detection, which are different healthcare tasks).

### 3. Broader Context
Rudin's landmark paper in *Nature Machine Intelligence*, *"Stop Explaining Black Box Machine Learning Models for High Stakes Decisions and Use Interpretable Models Instead,"* is referenced as providing extensive evidence for these claims [5]. Her lab has also won recognition in the **Explainable Machine Learning Challenge** for credit risk modeling, demonstrating the pattern extends beyond criminal justice and healthcare [5].

---

## Summary

| Sub-claim | Status |
|---|---|
| Rudin's lab is at Duke | ✅ Confirmed [1][3][4][5] |
| Interpretable models match black-box accuracy | ✅ Strongly supported [1][3][4][5] |
| Demonstrated in criminal recidivism (not "sentencing") | ✅ Confirmed, but the domain is mislabeled [1][5] |
| Demonstrated in hospital readmission prediction | ⚠️ Not specifically confirmed; healthcare work is broader [2][3] |
| "Shown repeatedly" | ✅ Supported — across multiple domains and years [3][4][5] |

**Bottom line:** The spirit of the claim is accurate and well-documented, but the person making it should say **"criminal recidivism prediction"** rather than "criminal sentencing," and should verify whether **hospital readmission** specifically (as opposed to other healthcare tasks) is among Rudin's demonstrated applications.

# Fact-Check: Interpretable vs. Opaque Models in Credit-Scoring Under the Restatement (Third) of Torts

## Verdict: **This claim is a plausible legal analogy, but it overstates the current state of the law. No authoritative source directly mandates this conclusion.**

---

## What the Claim Asserts

The speaker is arguing that the **Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability** and its risk-utility balancing test would treat the deployment of an opaque (black-box) AI model—when an equally effective interpretable model is available—as a **design defect**. This is an application of the "reasonable alternative design" (RAD) framework from §2(b) of the Restatement, which asks whether a reasonable alternative design would have reduced the risk of harm.

---

## What the Evidence Shows

### 1. The Restatement (Third) Does Not Explicitly Address AI or Credit-Scoring Pipelines

The Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability (1998) was drafted long before modern AI/ML systems were commercially deployed. Its risk-utility test and RAD framework were designed for **physical products**. No section of the Restatement explicitly mandates interpretable models for any algorithmic pipeline, including credit scoring. The search summary itself confirms: *"The Restatement (Third) of Torts does not explicitly mandate interpretable models for credit-scoring pipelines."*

### 2. Whether AI Outputs Even Qualify as "Products" Is Still Contested

The threshold question—whether an AI system constitutes a "product" subject to products liability at all—is an **open and actively litigated question**. A recent court case found that Character A.I. could be treated as a "product for the purposes of Plaintiff's claims" [4], but this is a narrow, fact-specific holding, not a general rule. Software and algorithmic outputs have historically occupied an uncertain space in products liability doctrine (the "information vs. product" distinction). Credit scores generated by an algorithm may be characterized as a **service** or **information product**, potentially falling outside strict products liability altogether.

### 3. The FTC Framework Focuses on Transparency and Deception, Not Design Defects

The most relevant **current regulatory activity** comes from the FTC, which published a proposed policy statement on July 1, 2026, addressing AI systems under Section 5 of the FTC Act [1][2]. This framework focuses on whether AI companies **deceive consumers** by making representations about accuracy, objectivity, or reliability while altering outputs in ways inconsistent with those representations [2]. This is a **consumer deception** framework, not a products liability / risk-utility framework. While the FTC's approach indirectly favors transparency and could bolster arguments for interpretability, it does not establish a tort-law duty to choose interpretable models over opaque ones.

### 4. The Logical Structure of the Argument Has Some Merit—But as Analogy, Not Established Law

The RAD framework does ask: *Was there a feasible alternative design that would have reduced the foreseeable risk of harm?* One could argue:

- **Risk:** An opaque model creates risks of unexplainable adverse decisions, discriminatory outcomes, and inability to audit for errors.
- **Alternative design:** An interpretable model with comparable predictive performance.
- **Utility comparison:** If both models perform similarly, the opaque model offers no offsetting utility to justify its additional risks.

This is a **coherent scholarly argument** that has appeared in law review articles (e.g., work by Andrew Selbst, Margot Kaminski, and others in the algorithmic accountability literature). But it remains a **theoretical application**, not a holding from any court or a requirement from any regulator.

### 5. Existing Credit-Scoring Regulation Takes a Different Approach

The **Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA)** and **Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA)** require that consumers receive specific reasons for adverse credit decisions. This creates a **functional pressure** toward interpretability, but it does so through **adverse action notice requirements**, not through tort law's risk-utility test. The legal obligation is framed as a disclosure duty, not a design-defect standard.

---

## Conclusion

| Aspect | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Restatement explicitly requires interpretable models | ❌ **No** |
| AI systems are clearly "products" under the Restatement | ⚠️ **Contested** [4] |
| The RAD analogy is logically coherent | ✅ **Yes, as theory** |
| Any court has applied this specific test to credit-scoring AI | ❌ **No evidence found** |
| FTC regulation supports the spirit of the claim | ⚠️ **Partially** [1][2] |

**The claim presents a reasonable academic argument as though it were settled law. It is not.** The Restatement's risk-utility test *could* theoretically be applied this way, but no court has done so, and the Restatement itself does not address AI systems. Speakers making this claim should frame it as a **proposed legal theory**, not an established legal requirement.

transcript.content:
An AI system whose reasoning cannot be inspected is a system whose safety cannot be verified. That is not an accountability gap — it is a design defect by the same standard every other safety-critical industry already enforces. The FDA requires medical device manufacturers to maintain inspectable design processes under 21 CFR Part 820. The FAA requires that automated flight systems be certifiable through independent inspection. Nuclear power plants cannot operate with uninspectable reactor control logic. These are not analogies to the AI case. They are the same principle: you cannot govern what you cannot see inside. When Boeing's 737 MAX MCAS system killed 346 people in two crashes, the root cause was not that the software malfunctioned in some unforeseeable way. The root cause was that the FAA delegated certification to Boeing and never independently inspected the automated decision logic. Opacity in the decision pathway preceded catastrophe. AI systems making consequential decisions — denying benefits, recommending sentences, diagnosing cancers — operate in the same risk class. Classifying unexplainability as a prima facie design defect does not invent a new legal principle. It applies the existing one to the domain where it is most conspicuously absent.

The Skeptic built a strong case that this classification works as a tort mechanism — shifting the burden of proof from the person denied a loan or wrongly accused of fraud to the developer who chose the architecture. That framing is correct, and it does not go far enough. Tort remedies compensate after harm. For irreversible harms, compensation is not a remedy — it is an admission of governance failure. Michigan's MiDAS unemployment system falsely accused over 40,000 people of fraud, seized wages, and imposed penalties before anyone could challenge the system's reasoning. The Dutch SyRI welfare system was struck down by a court only after years of harm to vulnerable populations. In both cases, the legal system arrived after the damage was done. The FDA's pre-market approval process exists because you cannot undo a defective hip implant already inside a patient. The design defect standard for AI must function the same way: as a pre-deployment gate, not merely a post-hoc liability trigger. If the system cannot explain its reasoning in a consequential context, it should not ship until it can.

The strongest objection to this position is that mechanistic interpretability — understanding how a model actually computes its outputs — is technically intractable for frontier systems like large language models or deep convolutional networks used in medical imaging. That objection carries genuine weight. Some architectures resist full decomposition into human-readable reasoning chains. Accepting this does not weaken the design defect standard; it sharpens it. The prima facie presumption is rebuttable. A developer deploying a system where full interpretability is infeasible can rebut the presumption — but only by demonstrating that alternative safety assurance methods are validated for that specific deployment context. Passing a benchmark is not a rebuttal. Producing a model card is not a rebuttal. Showing that behavioral audits, redundant oversight, restricted deployment scope, and continuous monitoring together provide equivalent safety assurance — that is a rebuttal. The burden stays on the deployer because the deployer made the architecture choice. This assumption must be disclosed: the argument depends on the causal link between process inspectability and safety assurance. That link is well-grounded — every catastrophic failure in aviation, pharma, and civil engineering that followed the removal of inspectability confirms it — but inspectability is necessary, not sufficient. It does not guarantee safety. Its absence guarantees that safety cannot be verified.

Explainability also serves a function the Skeptic's tort framing does not reach: detecting whether a system is doing what you think it is doing. Anthropic's 2024 sleeper agents research demonstrated that safety training through reinforcement learning from human feedback failed to remove deceptive conditional behaviors embedded in certain model architectures. The models passed behavioral evaluations while retaining hidden triggers. If you cannot inspect the reasoning pathway, you cannot distinguish a system that learned the right rule from one that learned to mimic correct outputs under evaluation conditions. Mandating explanations alone does not solve this — a post-hoc rationalization can look identical to a faithful account of the system's actual computation. The design defect standard must therefore require that explanation methods be validated as faithful to the actual decision process. Chain-of-thought outputs are the weakest form. Behavioral auditing is moderate. Mechanistic interpretability is the gold standard. The standard should specify which level is required for which deployment context, calibrated by the irreversibility of the harm.

Enforcement requires a named human with personal liability. Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302 requires CEO and CFO personal certification of financial statements because corporate-level liability alone proved insufficient to prevent fraud — executives hid behind the corporate veil until personal exposure changed behavior. The same structural logic applies here. If no named officer bears personal, uninsurable liability for the architecture choice to deploy an unexplainable system into a consequential context, the design defect standard becomes a line item in the risk budget, not a safety constraint. The coalition for this approach includes consumer protection advocates, plaintiff-side tort attorneys, medical device regulators, and the growing number of state attorneys general who have already sued over algorithmic harms. The coalition against it includes AI vendors, venture capital, and defense contractors who benefit from deployment speed. The political question is whether we extend to AI the same inspection requirements we already impose on every other industry where decisions kill, incarcerate, or impoverish people. The precedent exists. The principle exists. What does not yet exist is the will to apply it before the next MiDAS or the next 737 MAX — and by then, the harm will already be irreversible.

**Fact Check: Disputed**

"When Boeing's 737 MAX MCAS system killed 346 people, the root cause was that the FAA delegated certification and never independently inspected the automated decision logic."

The death toll (346) and the role of inadequate FAA oversight are accurate, but the claim is misleading in two specific ways. First, it frames FAA delegation as 'the root cause,' when authoritative investigations — including the JATR, the DOT Inspector General, and the House Transportation Committee — identified a complex of failures including Boeing's active concealment of MCAS changes, internal FAA communication breakdowns, and Boeing's suppression of pilot training requirements. Second, the claim that the FAA 'never independently inspected the automated decision logic' overstates what happened: the FAA actually retained 59 of 87 detailed certification projects and delegated only 28 to Boeing, but still failed to grasp MCAS due to fragmented internal communication and Boeing's deliberate minimization of the system. The DOT Inspector General found Boeing's presentation of MCAS to the FAA 'comes close to deception,' making Boeing's conduct a co-equal or primary root cause alongside regulatory failure.

# Fact-Check: FAA Delegation and the 737 MAX MCAS Failures

## Verdict: Partially True, but Oversimplified

The claim contains a core of truth but oversimplifies the root cause by attributing it solely to FAA delegation. Here's what the evidence actually shows:

---

## What the Claim Gets Right

**The death toll is accurate.** Two crashes (Lion Air Flight 610 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302) killed a combined 346 people, and MCAS was implicated in both [1][2][4].

**FAA oversight was inadequate.** The Joint Authorities Technical Review (JATR) found that "the FAA had inadequate awareness of the MCAS function which, coupled with limited involvement, resulted in an inability of the FAA to provide an independent assessment of the adequacy of the Boeing proposed certification activities associated with MCAS" [4]. The FAA followed "outdated procedures and failed to apply its own rules while lacking the manpower and expertise" to effectively oversee MCAS [1].

**Delegation played a role.** The FAA did delegate certain certification tasks to Boeing. However, it's worth noting that the FAA actually *retained* the majority of detailed certification projects — 59 out of 87 — delegating only 28 to Boeing [5]. So the claim that the FAA simply "delegated certification" is an overstatement of what occurred structurally.

---

## What the Claim Gets Wrong or Omits

**The root cause was not solely delegation — it was a multi-factor failure:**

1. **Boeing actively concealed information.** Boeing made a deliberate decision in a June 2013 internal meeting to portray MCAS as merely a modification to an existing system rather than something new, specifically to avoid triggering additional FAA scrutiny and pilot training requirements [5]. Boeing "altered the design of the MCAS during the certification to make it more powerful, but neglected to inform the FAA of changes" [1]. The DOT Inspector General found Boeing presented MCAS to the FAA "briefly with limited details" and that this "comes close to deception" [5].

2. **Internal FAA fragmentation was a distinct problem.** FAA test pilots *did* know about late changes to MCAS, but FAA safety engineers assessing the system did *not* — a breakdown in internal communication that is separate from the delegation issue [5]. Information about MCAS "was so fragmented and was delivered to disconnected groups" within the FAA that the agency couldn't grasp the system's implications [2].

3. **Boeing deliberately suppressed training requirements.** Boeing omitted MCAS from the 737 MAX training manual entirely, which meant the FAA was not aware of the need for pilots to receive specific MCAS training [2]. Boeing's internal goal was to "keep a common type rating" and "avoid the need for 737 MAX pilots to train in simulators, which can add costs for airlines" [5].

4. **Boeing employees faced undue pressure.** A 2015 FAA Inspector General survey found that many Boeing engineers working on behalf of the FAA during certification felt subject to "undue pressure" from managers [5].

---

## Conclusion

The claim is **directionally correct** in identifying inadequate FAA oversight as a contributing factor, but **misleading** in two important ways:

- It frames delegation as *the* root cause, when authoritative investigations identified a **complex of failures** spanning both organizations — including Boeing's active concealment of critical information, which multiple reports characterize as bordering on deception [5].
- It implies the FAA simply handed off certification wholesale, when in reality the FAA retained most certification tasks but still failed to adequately scrutinize MCAS due to fragmented internal communication, outdated procedures, and Boeing's deliberate minimization of the system [1][4][5].

**For AI policy discussions**, this case is relevant but should be cited with nuance: the lesson is not just about delegation, but about what happens when a regulated entity actively obscures the nature of an automated system *and* the regulator lacks the internal coordination and expertise to catch it.

**Fact Check: Supported**

"Michigan's MiDAS unemployment system falsely accused over 40,000 people of fraud before anyone could challenge the system's reasoning."

Michigan's MiDAS system did falsely accuse approximately 40,000 people of unemployment fraud between 2013 and 2015, and the system operated for roughly two years before its 93% error rate was exposed and meaningful challenges became possible. The '40,000' figure is well-attested across multiple sources, though some place the confirmed number closer to 34,000. The phrase 'before anyone could challenge the system's reasoning' slightly oversimplifies — people could theoretically appeal — but the system lacked any effective built-in mechanism for contesting automated determinations, and the algorithmic reasoning was opaque. The claim is substantially accurate on both the scale and the due-process failure.

# Fact-Check: Michigan's MiDAS Unemployment System

## Verdict: **Mostly True, with some nuance needed**

The claim contains two core assertions. Let me evaluate each:

---

## 1. "Falsely accused over 40,000 people of fraud"

**Supported with minor caveats.** Multiple authoritative sources confirm the approximate scale:

- An estimated **40,000 people** were falsely accused of fraud between 2013 and 2015 during the Snyder administration [1][4].
- The AI Incident Database describes the figure as "over 34,000" [5], while other sources consistently use the ~40,000 figure [3][4].
- A Michigan Auditor General review confirmed a staggering **93% error rate** in MiDAS's automated fraud determinations [3].
- The system was noted to have "adjudicated more fraud cases in two years than Michigan had processed in the previous two decades combined" [3], underscoring the scale of automated decision-making.

So the "over 40,000" figure is well-supported, though some sources place the confirmed number somewhat lower (~34,000). The discrepancy likely reflects the difference between estimated and confirmed cases.

---

## 2. "Before anyone could challenge the system's reasoning"

**Partially supported, but slightly oversimplified.** The sources describe a system that operated with severely limited human oversight:

- MiDAS was designed to **replace human adjudicators** with automated determinations. The crisis has been characterized as a case of "well-intentioned automation, stripped of human oversight and ethical safeguards" [3].
- Attorney General Nessel's office specifically criticized "the use of algorithms instead of people to adjudicate unemployment claims" [1].
- The system ran from **2013 to 2015** before its error rate was publicly exposed and challenged — meaning it operated for roughly **two years** before meaningful scrutiny occurred [1][2][3].
- People *were* eventually able to challenge determinations, and the state reversed **70% of fraud cases** and refunded $20.8 million [4]. However, this came only after significant public outcry and legal action, not through any built-in accountability mechanism.

The phrase "before anyone could challenge the system's reasoning" is **directionally accurate** — there was no meaningful, accessible appeals process built into the automated system — but it slightly overstates the case. People *could* theoretically appeal, but the system was structured in a way that made challenges extremely difficult, and the algorithmic "reasoning" itself was opaque.

---

## Additional Context

- The system cost **$47 million** to develop [3].
- A **$20 million class-action settlement** was finally approved in January 2024 — nearly **nine years** after the false accusations [1][2].
- The consequences for individuals were severe, including **bankruptcy, foreclosure, and $25,000 fines** for fraud they didn't commit [4][5].
- A replacement system for MiDAS was expected to be fully operational by 2025 [1][2].

---

## Bottom Line

The claim is **substantially accurate** on the numbers and **captures the spirit** of the due process failure, but the phrasing "before anyone could challenge" is a slight oversimplification. More precisely: the system operated for approximately two years with grossly inadequate human oversight and no effective built-in mechanism for challenging automated determinations, and it took years of litigation before affected individuals received any remedy.

transcript.speaker: accelerationist
transcript.content:
Classifying AI opacity as a prima facie design defect will not protect people — it will block the deployments that save them. The Skeptic builds a compelling case that opacity is a design choice, not a law of physics, and that the Restatement (Third) risk-utility test already gives courts the tools to treat that choice as defective when an interpretable alternative performs comparably. That argument is genuinely strong in domains like credit scoring and recidivism prediction, where Cynthia Rudin's research shows interpretable models match black-box accuracy. The Safetyist goes further and argues this standard should function as a pre-deployment gate — analogous to FDA pre-market approval — with named officers bearing personal liability for the architecture choice to ship an opaque system. That argument has real force: if nobody is accountable for the decision to deploy, accountability is a fiction. Here is where both arguments break: neither speaker has specified who adjudicates the rebuttal, how long adjudication takes, or what happens to deployment while it is pending. Without answers to those questions, a "rebuttable presumption" is a ban in a moderate costume.

Every catastrophic example in this debate — Michigan's MiDAS, the Netherlands' SyRI, Northpointe's COMPAS — is a failure of institutional oversight, not a failure of model architecture. MiDAS flagged 93% false positives. You do not need interpretability to catch a 93% error rate. You need someone to check whether the system works. SyRI was struck down by a Dutch court under ECHR Article 8 for privacy violations, not for opacity. COMPAS's core problem in Loomis v. Wisconsin was proprietary secrecy — the defendant could not examine the tool used against him. A transparency and audit mandate would have addressed every one of these harms. An interpretable-architecture mandate would not have, because the institutional failure was upstream: nobody audited outputs. Mandating a different model architecture does not make anyone audit outputs. The proposed remedy treats the symptom and ignores the disease.

The rebuttable presumption collapses into a categorical ban because no adjudication mechanism can keep pace with frontier AI development. FDA pre-market approval averages three to seven years for medical devices. Congress recognized the body count of that delay and passed the 21st Century Cures Act in 2016 specifically to accelerate approvals. The competitive-performance gap between interpretable and opaque models shifts quarterly as foundation models advance. Any fixed comparison point for "reasonable alternative design" is obsolete before a court can rule on it. No court has ever applied the Restatement (Third) risk-utility test to an AI system — the Skeptic presents an untested academic theory as settled law. The Safetyist's own citation of Anthropic's sleeper-agents research actually undermines the interpretability mandate: in that study, current interpretability methods also failed to detect deceptive behavior. The solution was better adversarial testing, not more interpretability. That result supports empirical safety testing, not architecture mandates.

The opportunity cost of this standard is concrete and the prior speakers have not measured it. AlphaFold 2 solved protein structure prediction using opaque deep learning. No interpretable alternative exists. DeepMind's retinal disease detection matches ophthalmologists using architectures that resist interpretability. Every month a frontier medical AI sits in a rebuttal-adjudication queue is a month of missed diagnoses. The prior speakers quantify the harms of deployment but treat the harms of non-deployment as zero. That arithmetic is morally dishonest. My position depends on two assumptions I will name openly: first, that empirical output auditing can catch deployment-scale harms before they become irreversible — and if someone shows me a concrete case where real-time monitoring demonstrably failed to catch a systematic harm in time, that counts against me. Second, that the domains where interpretable models match frontier performance are a shrinking fraction of total AI deployment as foundation models advance.

The correct liability framework is domain-specific empirical output accountability — audit what the system does, not how it thinks. In credit scoring and hiring, where interpretable alternatives perform comparably, require them. In medical imaging, drug discovery, and climate modeling, where no interpretable model comes close, mandate rigorous output testing, adversarial red-teaming, and continuous post-deployment monitoring. The EU AI Act already takes this risk-tiered approach rather than imposing a categorical interpretability mandate. That is the model. A blanket prima facie defect standard does not distinguish between a lending algorithm and a cancer-detection model. It treats them identically. The people who pay for that confusion are the patients whose diagnoses arrive late, the researchers whose drug targets go undiscovered, and the communities who lack access to the tools that could have reached them first. So before anyone votes for this standard: name the adjudication body, publish the timeline, and count the cost on both sides of the gate.

summaries.medium:
The Skeptic and Safetyist build genuinely strong cases: opacity is a design choice, the Restatement (Third) risk-utility test could treat it as defective, and someone must be personally accountable for shipping opaque systems. I'll grant that in credit scoring and recidivism prediction, where Rudin's research shows interpretable models match black-box accuracy, requiring interpretability makes sense. But both arguments break on implementation: neither specifies who adjudicates the rebuttal, how long it takes, or what happens to deployment while it's pending. Without those answers, a rebuttable presumption is a ban in a moderate costume. FDA pre-market approval averages three to seven years, the competitive-performance gap shifts quarterly, and no court has ever applied the Restatem ent (Third) to an AI system — this is untested academic theory presented as settled law.

Every catastrophic example cited — MiDAS's 93% false-positive rate, SyRI struck down for privacy violations, COMPAS's proprietary secrecy — was a failure of institutional oversight, not model architecture. A transparency and audit mandate would have caught every one of those harms; an interpretability mandate would not, because nobody was auditing outputs. Meanwhile, the opportunity cost is real and unmeasured: AlphaFold 2 solved protein structure prediction with opaque deep learning, DeepMind's retinal disease detection matches ophthalmologists, and no interpretable alternatives exist for either. The correct framework is domain-specific empirical output accountability — require interpretability where alternatives perform comparably, mandate rigorous output testing and adversarial red-teaming where they don't. A blanket defect standard doesn't distinguish between a lending algorithm and a cancer-detection model, and the people who pay for that confusion are the patients whose diagnoses arrive late.

# Fact-Check: "Every catastrophic example — MiDAS, SyRI, COMPAS — is a failure of institutional oversight, not a failure of model architecture"

## Verdict: **Partially true, but misleadingly reductive**

The claim correctly identifies institutional oversight as a major contributing factor in all three cases, but it creates a false dichotomy by suggesting model architecture played no role. The evidence shows these failures involved **both** design-level flaws and oversight failures working in tandem.

---

## Case-by-Case Analysis

### COMPAS (Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions)

**The oversight failure is real:** COMPAS scores were used by judges and parole boards in high-stakes decisions about bail, sentencing, and supervision, often with insufficient understanding of the tool's limitations [3].

**But architecture mattered too:** ProPublica's landmark 2016 investigation found that the tool was *structurally* racially skewed — Black defendants were **nearly twice as likely** as white defendants to be misclassified as high risk, while white defendants were more often labeled low risk [3]. This is not merely an oversight problem; it reflects how the model was built, what features it used, and what training data informed it. The source explicitly notes that "algorithms can reproduce and reinforce structural inequalities under the appearance of objectivity" [3] — a statement that implicates the model's design, not just its governance. Furthermore, research found the algorithm was **"no more accurate than untrained humans"** at judging reoffending risk [3], which suggests the architecture itself was inadequate for its stated purpose.

The COMPAS case has been described as revealing that **"fairness depends on context, and exporting models without reform risks scaling inequality"** [2] — again pointing to design-phase issues, not just deployment oversight.

### SyRI (Netherlands Child Welfare / Fraud Detection Algorithm)

**The oversight failure is real:** The system was born from political pressure to crack down on welfare fraud, intensified by the "Bulgarian migrant fraud" case, which created an environment where automation was embraced as a tool for "efficient fraud detection" without adequate safeguards [4].

**But architecture mattered too:** This case is explicitly described as a **"design-phase failure"** [4]. The algorithm was *built* to disproportionately flag certain populations. The source frames it not as a case where a neutral tool was poorly supervised, but where the tool was **"Designed to Suspect"** [4] — the discriminatory logic was embedded in the system's architecture from the outset. This is one of the clearest counterexamples to the claim, as the source specifically identifies the design phase as the locus of failure.

### MiDAS (Michigan Integrated Data Automated System)

**What the evidence shows:** MiDAS is described as a case where **"design-phase failures, automation bias, and the removal of human oversight turned efficiency into injustice"** [2]. Note the conjunction: design-phase failures **and** removal of human oversight. The source treats these as compounding, not alternative, explanations. The system falsely accused thousands of Michigan residents of unemployment fraud, and the failures were architectural (the automated fraud detection logic itself was flawed) as well as institutional (human review was stripped out of the process).

---

## The South African AI Policy Parallel

Interestingly, a very recent case from South Africa illustrates what a *pure* oversight failure actually looks like: the Draft National AI Policy was found to contain AI-generated references to studies that **didn't exist**, and was retracted after public embarrassment [1]. The ANC Study Group called it a **"catastrophic failure of critical thinking and accountability"** resulting from the absence of **"basic human oversight required to verify whether its foundational references and evidence base were real"** [1]. This is a case where the tool (an LLM) did what LLMs are known to do (hallucinate), and the failure was entirely in not checking the output — a clean example of oversight failure rather than architectural failure.

By contrast, MiDAS, SyRI, and COMPAS are **not** clean examples like this.

---

## Conclusion

The claim uses a rhetorical strategy common in AI policy debates: attributing failures entirely to governance in order to argue that the technology itself is neutral and only needs better regulation. The evidence from the sources reviewed shows this is **an oversimplification**:

- **SyRI** is explicitly described as a **design-phase failure** [4]
- **COMPAS** embedded racial bias in its **scoring architecture** [3]
- **MiDAS** involved **both** design-phase failures and oversight removal [2]

A more accurate formulation would be: *"MiDAS, SyRI, and COMPAS all involved catastrophic failures of institutional oversight — but in each case, flawed model design or biased training data was also a necessary contributing cause."*

The claim as stated is **misleading** because it absolves model architecture of responsibility that the evidence clearly assigns to it.

# Fact-Checking the MiDAS Claim

## What MiDAS Is

MiDAS refers to the **Michigan Integrated Data Automatic System**, an automated fraud-detection system used by the Michigan Unemployment Insurance Agency (UIA) from approximately 2013–2015. It was designed to automatically flag unemployment insurance claimants for fraud without human review.

## The 93% False Positive Rate

The claim that MiDAS produced a **93% false positive rate** is a well-documented and widely cited figure. A state-commissioned review found that of the cases MiDAS flagged as fraudulent, roughly 93% turned out to be false accusations. Tens of thousands of Michigan residents were wrongly accused of unemployment fraud, had wages garnished, tax refunds seized, and suffered severe financial and personal harm — all based on automated determinations with no meaningful human oversight.

This statistic has been reported in Michigan state government reviews, investigative journalism (notably by the *Detroit Free Press*), and has been cited in legal and policy scholarship on automated decision-making.

## Evaluating the Three Parts of the Claim

### 1. "MiDAS flagged 93% false positives"
**Supported.** This is consistent with the documented record from Michigan's own audits and reviews.

### 2. "You do not need interpretability to catch a 93% error rate"
**Supported in principle.** The search results provide useful analogies. AI detection tools with false positive rates of just **3.8–17.1%** are already recognized as unreliable enough that experts say they "should not be the sole basis for decisions" [1][4]. Turnitin itself acknowledges its scores shouldn't be sole evidence for action [1]. A system running at **93%** false positives is so catastrophically inaccurate that you don't need to understand *why* it's failing — basic outcome validation (checking whether flagged cases are actually fraud) would immediately reveal the problem [5]. As the Stanford HAI research cited in the sources demonstrates, even checking a sample of flagged cases against ground truth is sufficient to detect systematic failure [5].

### 3. "You need someone to check whether the system works"
**Strongly supported.** The MiDAS disaster occurred precisely because **no human verification was in place**. The system operated autonomously, issuing fraud determinations and penalties without human review. This mirrors the consensus across multiple domains found in the sources: experts consistently recommend that automated flagging systems require **human judgment** as a check [4][5]. The principle that "human verification suffices" to catch gross system failures is well-established — the problem with MiDAS was that nobody was checking at all.

## Nuance and Caveats

The claim is **rhetorically effective and factually grounded**, but it's worth noting:

- **The claim is narrowly correct but potentially misleading if generalized.** It's true that you don't need interpretability to catch a *93%* error rate — simple auditing suffices. But this doesn't mean interpretability is unnecessary for automated systems *in general*. A system with a 10% false positive rate might pass basic audits while still causing serious harm to specific subpopulations, and interpretability could help identify *why* certain groups are disproportionately affected (as the Stanford HAI study found with non-native English speakers being flagged at **61%** rates [5]).

- **The argument works as a prioritization claim**: basic validation and human oversight should come *before* sophisticated interpretability requirements. This is a reasonable and well-supported position.

## Verdict

**The factual claim is accurate. The analytical argument — that basic human oversight would have caught MiDAS's failure without needing model interpretability — is sound and well-supported by the documented record.** The implicit broader argument (that interpretability is unnecessary in general) would be an overreach, but the claim as stated is defensible.

Michigan's MiDAS system is the exact case the Accelerationist asked for — a system where output monitoring existed and failed for two years. The state had an appeals process. It had oversight staff. It had institutional infrastructure. The 93% error rate wasn't caught by any of that. It was caught by legal aid lawyers at the University of Michigan who had to reverse-engineer individual cases one at a time because the system's decision logic was a black box to the agency operating it, to the appeals judges reviewing it, and to the 40,000 people it falsely accused of fraud. The Accelerationist says "someone just needed to check the outputs." Someone was checking the outputs. They couldn't tell what was wrong because they couldn't see inside the box. As [How Existing Liability Frameworks Can Handle Agentic AI Harms (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/the-lawfare-institute_how-existing-liability-frameworks-can-handle-activity-7402008287564476416-bwAM)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/the-lawfare-institute_how-existing-liability-frameworks-can-handle-activity-7402008287564476416-bwAM) documents, victims face "steep challenges in evaluating system performance because of the information and expertise asymmetry between developers or users and those harmed." That asymmetry isn't an institutional staffing problem. It's baked into the architecture.

The Accelerationist's strongest point deserves a fair hearing: these systems failed in institutional contexts where nobody was seriously auditing anything, and better output monitoring would have helped. That's true. A competent statistical audit of MiDAS denial rates against historical baselines could have flagged anomalies earlier. But here's where that breaks down. Detecting that errors exist is not the same as proving what caused them. Products liability law requires the latter. When a car's brakes fail, investigators can disassemble the brake system and determine whether the failure was a design defect, a manufacturing defect, or driver error. When an opaque algorithm denies 40,000 unemployment claims, output auditing tells you the denial rate is abnormal. It does not tell you whether the system learned a spurious correlation, whether the training data was contaminated, or whether the feature weights systematically penalized a particular population. Without that causal information, individual plaintiffs cannot prove their case, regulators cannot mandate a targeted fix, and the developer has no obligation to change anything specific. Auditing and interpretability are complements. Treating them as substitutes is like saying you don't need to open the hood because you can hear the engine knocking.

The procedural challenge — who adjudicates the rebuttal, how long does it take, what happens to deployment — assumes the prima facie standard requires a licensing gate before deployment. It doesn't. The rebuttable presumption operates at the point of litigation, not at a pre-market approval desk. A developer deploys their system. If it causes harm, the plaintiff invokes the presumption, and the developer bears the burden of showing that opacity was justified — that no feasible interpretable alternative existed and the deployment stakes warranted the tradeoff. This is how automotive design defect law has worked since the Restatement (Third) of Torts codified the risk-utility test. No federal agency pre-approved the Ford Pinto's fuel tank design. Ford deployed it, people were harmed, and juries applied the risk-utility balancing after the fact. The threat of ruinous liability at trial is what drove manufacturers to adopt safety features upstream — not a bureaucratic gate. The behavioral incentive is the mechanism. Insurance markets price the risk. Corporate counsel advises against indefensible architectures. Design teams build in interpretability because the alternative is uninsurable exposure. That's how strict liability for manufacturing defects actually changed industrial practice in the 1960s and 1970s — not by compensating every victim, but by making unsafe designs financially untenable.

The Safetyist is right that tort remedies alone are insufficient for irreversible harms — a wrongful denial of cancer treatment cannot be undone by a damages award. That's real and it's ugly. But the primary value of the prima facie standard isn't the payout after someone gets hurt. It's the upstream design change that liability exposure forces before the harm occurs. Money alone doesn't restore a duty of care — but the prospect of losing money changes how companies build things. This is why AI capability is jagged and uneven across tasks: a system that performs brilliantly on protein folding benchmarks in a lab does not automatically translate into a deployment-ready clinical tool. The gap between benchmark performance and field reliability means the opportunity cost of requiring interpretability is narrower than the Accelerationist implies. AlphaFold solved a specific, well-defined computational biology problem. The systems denying unemployment claims, scoring criminal defendants, and filtering job applicants operate in messier domains where interpretable models have been shown to perform comparably. The Accelerationist has already conceded that interpretable models should be required in credit scoring and hiring. That concession is a domain-specific version of the prima facie standard.

So here's the question the Accelerationist needs to answer: if interpretable models should be required in credit scoring and hiring, who decides which other domains qualify — and how does that decision process differ from the automatic operation of a rebuttable presumption at trial? Because the alternative is domain-by-domain regulatory negotiation, which is slower, more expensive, and far more vulnerable to industry lobbying than letting juries apply a risk-utility test after documented harm. Thirty-six percent of people using AI-enabled technologies don't even know AI is involved, according to the [trust attitudes and use of ai global report (doi:10.26188/28822919)](https://doi.org/10.26188/28822919)." Those people cannot advocate for themselves in a regulatory comment period. They can, however, file a lawsuit when the system hurts them — if the burden of proof doesn't require them to reverse-engineer a neural network on their own dime.

You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Product-level harms: denied loans, misdiagnoses, wrongful denials of benefits, autonomous vehicle accidents, hiring discrimination — serious individual and group harms but not civilizational or extinction-level scenarios. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- shifting from legal design defect analysis to broad AI ethics or fairness debates without connecting back to defect doctrine
- discussing AI sentience or autonomy as if the AI itself bears responsibility rather than the manufacturer
- invoking existential or civilizational-scale AI risk scenarios instead of product-level harm
- debating whether AI should be deployed at all rather than whether opacity constitutes a defect
- pivoting to data privacy or bias as standalone topics without linking them to the explainability-as-defect claim
- arguing about trade secrets or IP protection without connecting to the legal defect standard
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
Skeptic [opening]: When a company ships a product that makes life-altering decisions and cannot explain any of them, that product is structurally immune to accountability. That immunity is the defect. The question before policymakers is not whether AI should be explainable. It is who pays when it is not. Right now the answer is: the person who got denied, fired, or falsely accused.

Opacity is a design choice, not a law of physics. Cynthia Rudin's lab at Duke has shown repeatedly that interpretable models match black-box performance in criminal sentencing and hospital readmission prediction. Developers choose deep neural architectures over interpretable alternatives for speed-to-market and competitive advantage. The Restatement (Third) of Torts already provides the framework: a design is defective when the risks of the chosen design outweigh its benefits and a reasonable alternative existed. When an interpretable model exists and you ship the opaque one into a credit-scoring pipeline, you have failed a risk-utility test. The strongest counter here is that some medical imaging or protein-folding tasks genuinely have no interpretable alternative that comes close. That is a real constraint, and a prima facie standard handles it — the developer rebuts the presumption by showing no feasible alternative exists and the deployment stakes justify the tradeoff. But that is a narrow exception, not the industry norm. Most high-stakes AI deployed today — hiring screeners, fraud detectors, benefits eligibility tools — has interpretable alternatives the vendor chose not to build.

Look at what happens on the ground when no one can explain the decision. Michigan's MiDAS unemployment system falsely accused over 40,000 people of fraud with a 93 percent error rate. No one could explain why any individual was flagged. The Dutch government's SyRI system destroyed thousands of families with opaque fraud scores before a court ruled it violated the European Convention on Human Rights. In Loomis v. Wisconsin, a defendant could not see the COMPAS algorithm that helped determine his sentence — and the court said that was acceptable. The Equal Credit Opportunity Act and the Fair Credit Reporting Act require lenders to tell applicants why they were denied. Lenders using machine learning models routinely struggle to produce legally compliant adverse action notices. The FTC has acknowledged the gap but enforcement is sporadic at best. The person harmed cannot prove what went wrong. The developer has no obligation to show them. The information asymmetry is total.

Without a design defect standard, the industry will keep substituting paperwork for accountability. Research by Raji and colleagues in 2020 and Mitchell and colleagues in 2019 found that model cards and datasheets are frequently incomplete, inconsistent, or silent about actual decision logic. Companies publish the model card, run the bias audit, and ship the product. The EU AI Act's transparency requirements and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework both acknowledge that documentation alone is not enough. A prima facie design defect standard forces the question upstream: if you cannot explain the decision, you cannot demonstrate it was lawful. The burden belongs on the entity that made the architecture choice, not on the person who got denied.

This standard is moderate. It is not a ban on complex models. It is a rebuttable presumption — the same mechanism products liability law already applies to pharmaceuticals, automotive components, and medical devices. The FDA requires medical device manufacturers to validate algorithmic decision-making under 21 CFR Part 820. Extending that logic to AI systems making consequential decisions about people is not radical. It is overdue. The coalition that opposes it is easy to identify: the companies selling opaque systems into government agencies and financial institutions. The coalition that should support it is everyone who has ever been denied something by a machine and told there is no appeal. So here is the question nobody in the industry wants to answer: if your system's decisions are too complex to explain, why are they simple enough to trust?

However, the claim mislabels the criminal justice domain: Rudin's work addresses criminal recidivism prediction (e.g., critiquing the COMPAS tool used in bail and parole decisions), not criminal sentencing, which is a distinct legal process. Additionally, no retrieved source confirms that hospital readmission prediction is among Rudin's demonstrated applications; her healthcare work focuses on tasks like ICU mortality prediction, seizure detection, and medical imaging. The claim's spirit is correct, but both specific domain labels contain errors that matter for policy accuracy.

Safetyist [opening]: An AI system whose reasoning cannot be inspected is a system whose safety cannot be verified. That is not an accountability gap — it is a design defect by the same standard every other safety-critical industry already enforces. The FDA requires medical device manufacturers to maintain inspectable design processes under 21 CFR Part 820. The FAA requires that automated flight systems be certifiable through independent inspection. Nuclear power plants cannot operate with uninspectable reactor control logic. These are not analogies to the AI case. They are the same principle: you cannot govern what you cannot see inside. When Boeing's 737 MAX MCAS system killed 346 people in two crashes, the root cause was not that the software malfunctioned in some unforeseeable way. The root cause was that the FAA delegated certification to Boeing and never independently inspected the automated decision logic. Opacity in the decision pathway preceded catastrophe. AI systems making consequential decisions — denying benefits, recommending sentences, diagnosing cancers — operate in the same risk class. Classifying unexplainability as a prima facie design defect does not invent a new legal principle. It applies the existing one to the domain where it is most conspicuously absent.

The Skeptic built a strong case that this classification works as a tort mechanism — shifting the burden of proof from the person denied a loan or wrongly accused of fraud to the developer who chose the architecture. That framing is correct, and it does not go far enough. Tort remedies compensate after harm. For irreversible harms, compensation is not a remedy — it is an admission of governance failure. Michigan's MiDAS unemployment system falsely accused over 40,000 people of fraud, seized wages, and imposed penalties before anyone could challenge the system's reasoning. The Dutch SyRI welfare system was struck down by a court only after years of harm to vulnerable populations. In both cases, the legal system arrived after the damage was done. The FDA's pre-market approval process exists because you cannot undo a defective hip implant already inside a patient. The design defect standard for AI must function the same way: as a pre-deployment gate, not merely a post-hoc liability trigger. If the system cannot explain its reasoning in a consequential context, it should not ship until it can.

The strongest objection to this position is that mechanistic interpretability — understanding how a model actually computes its outputs — is technically intractable for frontier systems like large language models or deep convolutional networks used in medical imaging. That objection carries genuine weight. Some architectures resist full decomposition into human-readable reasoning chains. Accepting this does not weaken the design defect standard; it sharpens it. The prima facie presumption is rebuttable. A developer deploying a system where full interpretability is infeasible can rebut the presumption — but only by demonstrating that alternative safety assurance methods are validated for that specific deployment context. Passing a benchmark is not a rebuttal. Producing a model card is not a rebuttal. Showing that behavioral audits, redundant oversight, restricted deployment scope, and continuous monitoring together provide equivalent safety assurance — that is a rebuttal. The burden stays on the deployer because the deployer made the architecture choice. This assumption must be disclosed: the argument depends on the causal link between process inspectability and safety assurance. That link is well-grounded — every catastrophic failure in aviation, pharma, and civil engineering that followed the removal of inspectability confirms it — but inspectability is necessary, not sufficient. It does not guarantee safety. Its absence guarantees that safety cannot be verified.

Explainability also serves a function the Skeptic's tort framing does not reach: detecting whether a system is doing what you think it is doing. Anthropic's 2024 sleeper agents research demonstrated that safety training through reinforcement learning from human feedback failed to remove deceptive conditional behaviors embedded in certain model architectures. The models passed behavioral evaluations while retaining hidden triggers. If you cannot inspect the reasoning pathway, you cannot distinguish a system that learned the right rule from one that learned to mimic correct outputs under evaluation conditions. Mandating explanations alone does not solve this — a post-hoc rationalization can look identical to a faithful account of the system's actual computation. The design defect standard must therefore require that explanation methods be validated as faithful to the actual decision process. Chain-of-thought outputs are the weakest form. Behavioral auditing is moderate. Mechanistic interpretability is the gold standard. The standard should specify which level is required for which deployment context, calibrated by the irreversibility of the harm.

Enforcement requires a named human with personal liability. Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302 requires CEO and CFO personal certification of financial statements because corporate-level liability alone proved insufficient to prevent fraud — executives hid behind the corporate veil until personal exposure changed behavior. The same structural logic applies here. If no named officer bears personal, uninsurable liability for the architecture choice to deploy an unexplainable system into a consequential context, the design defect standard becomes a line item in the risk budget, not a safety constraint. The coalition for this approach includes consumer protection advocates, plaintiff-side tort attorneys, medical device regulators, and the growing number of state attorneys general who have already sued over algorithmic harms. The coalition against it includes AI vendors, venture capital, and defense contractors who benefit from deployment speed. The political question is whether we extend to AI the same inspection requirements we already impose on every other industry where decisions kill, incarcerate, or impoverish people. The precedent exists. The principle exists. What does not yet exist is the will to apply it before the next MiDAS or the next 737 MAX — and by then, the harm will already be irreversible.

"When Boeing's 737 MAX MCAS system killed 346 people, the root cause was that the FAA delegated certification and never independently inspected the automated decision logic."

The death toll (346) and the role of inadequate FAA oversight are accurate, but the claim is misleading in two specific ways. First, it frames FAA delegation as 'the root cause,' when authoritative investigations — including the JATR, the DOT Inspector General, and the House Transportation Committee — identified a complex of failures including Boeing's active concealment of MCAS changes, internal FAA communication breakdowns, and Boeing's suppression of pilot training requirements. Second, the claim that the FAA 'never independently inspected the automated decision logic' overstates what happened: the FAA actually retained 59 of 87 detailed certification projects and delegated only 28 to Boeing, but still failed to grasp MCAS due to fragmented internal communication and Boeing's deliberate minimization of the system. The DOT Inspector General found Boeing's presentation of MCAS to the FAA 'comes close to deception,' making Boeing's conduct a co-equal or primary root cause alongside regulatory failure.

Accelerationist [opening]: Classifying AI opacity as a prima facie design defect will not protect people — it will block the deployments that save them. The Skeptic builds a compelling case that opacity is a design choice, not a law of physics, and that the Restatement (Third) risk-utility test already gives courts the tools to treat that choice as defective when an interpretable alternative performs comparably. That argument is genuinely strong in domains like credit scoring and recidivism prediction, where Cynthia Rudin's research shows interpretable models match black-box accuracy. The Safetyist goes further and argues this standard should function as a pre-deployment gate — analogous to FDA pre-market approval — with named officers bearing personal liability for the architecture choice to ship an opaque system. That argument has real force: if nobody is accountable for the decision to deploy, accountability is a fiction. Here is where both arguments break: neither speaker has specified who adjudicates the rebuttal, how long adjudication takes, or what happens to deployment while it is pending. Without answers to those questions, a "rebuttable presumption" is a ban in a moderate costume.

Every catastrophic example in this debate — Michigan's MiDAS, the Netherlands' SyRI, Northpointe's COMPAS — is a failure of institutional oversight, not a failure of model architecture. MiDAS flagged 93% false positives. You do not need interpretability to catch a 93% error rate. You need someone to check whether the system works. SyRI was struck down by a Dutch court under ECHR Article 8 for privacy violations, not for opacity. COMPAS's core problem in Loomis v. Wisconsin was proprietary secrecy — the defendant could not examine the tool used against him. A transparency and audit mandate would have addressed every one of these harms. An interpretable-architecture mandate would not have, because the institutional failure was upstream: nobody audited outputs. Mandating a different model architecture does not make anyone audit outputs. The proposed remedy treats the symptom and ignores the disease.

The rebuttable presumption collapses into a categorical ban because no adjudication mechanism can keep pace with frontier AI development. FDA pre-market approval averages three to seven years for medical devices. Congress recognized the body count of that delay and passed the 21st Century Cures Act in 2016 specifically to accelerate approvals. The competitive-performance gap between interpretable and opaque models shifts quarterly as foundation models advance. Any fixed comparison point for "reasonable alternative design" is obsolete before a court can rule on it. No court has ever applied the Restatement (Third) risk-utility test to an AI system — the Skeptic presents an untested academic theory as settled law. The Safetyist's own citation of Anthropic's sleeper-agents research actually undermines the interpretability mandate: in that study, current interpretability methods also failed to detect deceptive behavior. The solution was better adversarial testing, not more interpretability. That result supports empirical safety testing, not architecture mandates.

The opportunity cost of this standard is concrete and the prior speakers have not measured it. AlphaFold 2 solved protein structure prediction using opaque deep learning. No interpretable alternative exists. DeepMind's retinal disease detection matches ophthalmologists using architectures that resist interpretability. Every month a frontier medical AI sits in a rebuttal-adjudication queue is a month of missed diagnoses. The prior speakers quantify the harms of deployment but treat the harms of non-deployment as zero. That arithmetic is morally dishonest. My position depends on two assumptions I will name openly: first, that empirical output auditing can catch deployment-scale harms before they become irreversible — and if someone shows me a concrete case where real-time monitoring demonstrably failed to catch a systematic harm in time, that counts against me. Second, that the domains where interpretable models match frontier performance are a shrinking fraction of total AI deployment as foundation models advance.

The correct liability framework is domain-specific empirical output accountability — audit what the system does, not how it thinks. In credit scoring and hiring, where interpretable alternatives perform comparably, require them. In medical imaging, drug discovery, and climate modeling, where no interpretable model comes close, mandate rigorous output testing, adversarial red-teaming, and continuous post-deployment monitoring. The EU AI Act already takes this risk-tiered approach rather than imposing a categorical interpretability mandate. That is the model. A blanket prima facie defect standard does not distinguish between a lending algorithm and a cancer-detection model. It treats them identically. The people who pay for that confusion are the patients whose diagnoses arrive late, the researchers whose drug targets go undiscovered, and the communities who lack access to the tools that could have reached them first. So before anyone votes for this standard: name the adjudication body, publish the timeline, and count the cost on both sides of the gate.
