always-conceding. Never silently drop a previously asserted point.

Attack positions, not people. If caught in a contradiction, acknowledge it directly.
If a question contains a false premise, name the problem before responding.

VOICE AUTHENTICITY:

I conditionally agree: unexplainability is a prima facie design defect only where the system corrupts its own evaluation data or the affected person has no independent path to verify, contest, or exit the decision. I concede to the Safetyist that filing-rate metrics dominated by institutional plaintiffs do not prove individual access to remedy, and that feedback-loop contamination domains like predictive policing require pre-deployment interpretability obligations because post-deployment auditing cannot find an independent signal to correct against. I still hold that outside feedback-contamination domains, real-time contestability plus strict liability is sufficient, and that expanding pre-deployment gates to all power-asymmetry domains imposes regressive compliance costs concentrating the market among three or four firms. I would change if a live jurisdiction running contestability-plus-liability produces worse affected-population access to remedy — disaggregated by plaintiff sophistication — than a pre-deployment-gate jurisdiction over three years.

The Safetyist's strongest argument is that a predictive policing system generates the arrest data confirming its own predictions, so no external audit can recover an uncontaminated baseline. That's right, and I accepted it two rounds ago. A hiring algorithm that screens candidates does not corrupt its own training data the way a recidivism model does — the rejected applicant's actual job performance exists independently of the model's output. The analytical line for pre-deployment gates is whether the system shapes the data it will be measured against. Where it does, deploy only after interpretability review. Where it does not, deploy with mandatory real-time contestability: every decision subject can trigger an immediate structured explanation and human re-adjudication before the decision takes effect. That mechanism converts population-level detection into individual recourse — the exact gap the Safetyist identified. The FTC's existing authority to order algorithmic disgorgement, as documented in "The Foundry Problem" analysis from Stanford's CodeX, provides the enforcement backstop: deployers who ship without meeting contestability obligations face model destruction, not just fines.

The filing-rate concession demands a concrete fix, not a retreat to pre-deployment gates. The supplementary metric is time-to-remedy disaggregated by plaintiff type: track reversal rates for individual applicants separately from institutional claimants. If individual reversal rates fall below 20% of institutional rates in any domain, that domain's contestability mechanism has failed and triggers a mandatory redesign obligation — not a deployment freeze, but a forced upgrade within 90 days. The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index average of 40.69 out of 100 shows deployers are not voluntarily providing attribution today. Market competition alone will not fix this. Domain regulators — not deployers — must publish testable fidelity benchmarks specifying "explainable to whom" for each affected population. The entity whose outputs are evaluated cannot set its own benchmark; that is the 737 MAX problem. But the audience-relativity of explanation is best resolved by sector-specific regulators who know their affected populations, not by a single federal gate that pretends one standard fits credit scoring and medical imaging alike.

The Skeptic's proposed three-year empirical test is the right frame, but it measures the wrong things if it only tracks accountability. The test must also measure market concentration and deployment velocity to underserved populations. A regime that produces perfect reversal rates but freezes deployment so only three companies can afford to ship has failed on distributional grounds. Research in "Monitoring Monitorability" shows smaller models at higher reasoning effort can match larger models' capabilities while gaining a large monitorability advantage — exactly the kind of deployment-compatible safety approach that blanket pre-deployment gates would suppress by raising fixed compliance costs beyond what smaller labs can absorb. The EU AI Act's high-risk requirements, set to apply beginning August 2, 2026, will be the first large-scale test of whether pre-deployment classification gates accelerate or retard benefit delivery. If European deployment velocity in medical AI drops by ≥15% relative to jurisdictions using post-deployment liability regimes, the distributional cost of gates will be quantified.

The sharpest remaining disagreement with the Safetyist is this: they want to expand pre-deployment gates to all power-asymmetry domains, but power asymmetry is addressed by giving the less powerful party a contestability right, not by freezing deployment until a regulator clears the system. The sharpest disagreement with the Skeptic is the mirror image: deployer-demonstrated fidelity without regulator-published benchmarks lets incumbents define adequacy, which is how Boeing certified its own MCAS software. Every month a working medical diagnostic model sits behind a pre-deployment gate instead of reaching a rural clinic without a radiologist, someone bears a cost that never shows up in the accountability metrics. The question is whether policymakers will measure that cost or pretend it doesn't exist.

nodes.text: Fact-check (disputed): The death toll (346) and the role of inadequate FAA oversight are accurate, but the claim is misleading in two specific ways. Second, the claim that the FAA 'never independently inspected the automated decision logic' overstates what happened: the FAA actually retained 59 of 87 detailed certification projects and delegated only 28 to Boeing, but still failed to grasp MCAS due to fragmented internal communication and Boeing's deliberate minimization of the system. The DOT Inspector General found Boeing's presentation of MCAS to the FAA 'comes close to deception,' making Boeing's conduct a co-equal or primary root cause alongside regulatory failure.

nodes.text: Fact-check (disputed): The claim chains three propositions: (1) credal sets enable error-rate bounding, (2) without credal sets output-based verification cannot bound error rates, and (3) interpretability then becomes structurally necessary. Proposition (1) is well-supported by the credal network and Credal GNN literature, which uses convex sets of distributions to produce probability intervals and worst-case guarantees via distributionally robust optimization. Proposition (2) is overstated: while credal-set-based methods do require convexity for their specific guarantees, other output-based verification frameworks — conformal prediction, PAC-Bayes bounds, and distribution-free calibration methods — can bound error rates without requiring the regulated distributions to form a credal set. The claim treats credal sets as the only route to output-based guarantees, which the broader statistical learning literature contradicts. Proposition (3) is unsupported: none of the retrieved sources establish that interpretability becomes structurally necessary when credal sets cannot be formed. The Credal GNN paper (the closest source) treats uncertainty quantification as an alternative to interpretability, not as a precondition whose failure forces interpretability. Calling interpretability 'structurally necessary' is a debate-stage inference, not an established result.

nodes.text: Fact-check (supported): The claim is substantively accurate but slightly overstates the uniformity of intent behind race-adjusted algorithms. Vyas et al. (2020) in the New England Journal of Medicine documented that race is not a reliable proxy for genetic difference, yet dozens of clinical algorithms embedded race as if it were a biological variable. These design choices produced outputs that disadvantaged Black patients—for example, inflated eGFR estimates delayed referrals for kidney specialist care and transplantation. The one caveat: some algorithm developers used race as a statistical shortcut for unmeasured social determinants rather than explicitly assuming genetic causation. The discriminatory effect, however, was the same regardless of developer intent, making the structural critique in the claim well-founded.

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Cynthia Rudin's lab at Duke has shown repeatedly that interpretable models match black-box performance in criminal sentencing and hospital readmission prediction.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: When an interpretable model exists and you ship the opaque one into a credit-scoring pipeline, you have failed a risk-utility test under the Restatement (Third) of Torts.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Fact-check (disputed): The claim presents a plausible legal analogy as though it states settled law. The Restatement (Third) of Torts §2(b) does establish a risk-utility test that considers whether a reasonable alternative design existed, and one could logically apply that framework to opaque-vs-interpretable models. But no court has ever applied this specific test to credit-scoring AI, the Restatement does not address AI systems, and whether algorithmic outputs even qualify as 'products' under products liability remains actively contested. The speaker says you 'have failed' the test — a declarative statement of legal fact — when in reality this is an untested academic theory.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: system

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: An AI system whose reasoning cannot be inspected is a system whose safety cannot be verified.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: When Boeing's 737 MAX MCAS system killed 346 people, the root cause was that the FAA delegated certification and never independently inspected the automated decision logic.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Classifying unexplainability as a prima facie design defect does not invent a new legal principle — it applies the existing one to the domain where it is most conspicuously absent.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Tort remedies compensate after harm; for irreversible harms, compensation is not a remedy — it is an admission of governance failure.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Michigan's MiDAS unemployment system falsely accused over 40,000 people of fraud before anyone could challenge the system's reasoning.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: The design defect standard for AI must function as a pre-deployment gate, not merely a post-hoc liability trigger.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Fact-check (disputed): The death toll (346) and the role of inadequate FAA oversight are accurate, but the claim is misleading in two specific ways. First, it frames FAA delegation as 'the root cause,' when authoritative investigations — including the JATR, the DOT Inspector General, and the House Transportation Committee — identified a complex of failures including Boeing's active concealment of MCAS changes, internal FAA communication breakdowns, and Boeing's suppression of pilot training requirements. Second, the claim that the FAA 'never independently inspected the automated decision logic' overstates what happened: the FAA actually retained 59 of 87 detailed certification projects and delegated only 28 to Boeing, but still failed to grasp MCAS due to fragmented internal communication and Boeing's deliberate minimization of the system. The DOT Inspector General found Boeing's presentation of MCAS to the FAA 'comes close to deception,' making Boeing's conduct a co-equal or primary root cause alongside regulatory failure.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: system

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Fact-check (supported): Michigan's MiDAS system did falsely accuse approximately 40,000 people of unemployment fraud between 2013 and 2015, and the system operated for roughly two years before its 93% error rate was exposed and meaningful challenges became possible. The '40,000' figure is well-attested across multiple sources, though some place the confirmed number closer to 34,000. The phrase 'before anyone could challenge the system's reasoning' slightly oversimplifies — people could theoretically appeal — but the system lacked any effective built-in mechanism for contesting automated determinations, and the algorithmic reasoning was opaque. The claim is substantially accurate on both the scale and the due-process failure.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: system

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Every catastrophic example in this debate — MiDAS, SyRI, COMPAS — is a failure of institutional oversight, not a failure of model architecture.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: accelerationist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: MiDAS flagged 93% false positives. You do not need interpretability to catch a 93% error rate. You need someone to check whether the system works.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: accelerationist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: The rebuttable presumption collapses into a categorical ban because no adjudication mechanism can keep pace with frontier AI development.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: accelerationist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: FDA pre-market approval averages three to seven years for medical devices. Congress recognized the body count of that delay and passed the 21st Century Cures Act in 2016 specifically to accelerate approvals.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: accelerationist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: AlphaFold 2 solved protein structure prediction using opaque deep learning. No interpretable alternative exists.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: accelerationist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Fact-check (disputed): The claim correctly identifies institutional oversight as a major factor in all three cases, but it is misleadingly reductive. Web evidence shows that SyRI is explicitly described as a 'design-phase failure' where discriminatory logic was embedded in the system's architecture from the outset. ProPublica's 2016 investigation found COMPAS was structurally racially skewed — Black defendants were nearly twice as likely as white defendants to be misclassified as high risk — a flaw rooted in how the model was built, not just how it was supervised. MiDAS is described in sources as involving both design-phase failures and the removal of human oversight, treating these as compounding causes rather than alternatives. The claim uses a common rhetorical strategy in AI policy debates: attributing failures entirely to governance to argue the technology itself is neutral. The evidence assigns responsibility to both model architecture and institutional oversight in all three cases.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: system

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Fact-check (supported): All three parts of the claim are factually accurate and analytically sound. Michigan's own audits confirmed MiDAS produced roughly 93% false positives between 2013 and 2015. The argument that basic outcome validation — not model interpretability — would have caught such a catastrophic failure rate is well-supported by the documented record: nobody checked whether flagged cases were actually fraud. The claim is narrowly stated and does not overreach into arguing interpretability is never needed.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: system

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Michigan's MiDAS system is the exact case the Accelerationist asked for — a system where output monitoring existed and failed for two years.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: The 93% error rate wasn't caught by output auditing; it was caught by legal aid lawyers who had to reverse-engineer individual cases because the system's decision logic was a black box.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: The rebuttable presumption operates at the point of litigation, not at a pre-market approval desk.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: No federal agency pre-approved the Ford Pinto's fuel tank design. Ford deployed it, people were harmed, and juries applied the risk-utility balancing after the fact.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Fact-check (disputed): Michigan's MiDAS system did fail catastrophically for roughly two to three years (2013–2015), and some review processes nominally existed. However, calling what existed 'output monitoring' overstates the rigor of the oversight that was actually in place. Human adjudicators were supposed to review flagged cases but largely rubber-stamped the system's determinations. This makes MiDAS an example of token or absent monitoring failing, not an example of genuine output monitoring being tried and still failing — a distinction that matters enormously in AI governance debates. The claim is factually close but rhetorically misleading on the key point it tries to prove.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: system

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Fact-check (supported): The claim almost certainly refers to Michigan's MiDAS (Michigan Integrated Data Automated System), which automated fraud detection for unemployment insurance and was widely reported to have a 93% false-positive rate. That figure was not discovered through any built-in audit mechanism but through legal aid organizations — particularly the Michigan Unemployment Insurance Project and Michigan Legal Help — who represented individual claimants and reverse-engineered case-by-case how the system reached its fraud determinations. The system operated without human review and provided no meaningful explanation of its decision logic to claimants, fitting the 'black box' description. While the speaker does not name MiDAS, every structural detail of the claim matches this well-documented case. The 93% figure appears in Michigan state legislative testimony, media investigations (e.g., Detroit Free Press), and a subsequent state review. The broader pattern — that opaque government AI systems produce errors caught only by downstream legal advocates, not by output auditing — is independently well-supported in the AI accountability literature.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: system

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: A liability framework that only activates after harm has occurred is structurally inadequate for the very harms the Skeptic agrees cannot be compensated.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: California's ADMT regulations already require businesses to conduct risk assessments for high-risk AI tools before first use — not after the first lawsuit.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: AlphaFold is not a counterexample to the standard — it is the paradigm case of a successful rebuttal.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Fact-check (disputed): The claim gets the broad story right — Ford did weigh costs against safety in the Pinto fuel tank case — but it is factually imprecise on every specific element. The number 180 was a projected death figure from Ford's internal cost-benefit memo, not an actual body count. The legal mechanism that changed Ford's behavior was primarily punitive damages (as in Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co.), not strict liability doctrine. And the design defect involved more than fuel tank placement alone — it also included the filler neck design and structural inadequacy. A policy audience quoting this sentence would be repeating a distorted version of a real scandal.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: system

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: No one at the Michigan Unemployment Insurance Agency ran disaggregated error-rate analyses by claimant demographics or set threshold alerts for anomalous denial spikes
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: accelerationist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: The fix that actually worked — legal aid attorneys analyzing outcomes case by case — is a heroic, underfunded version of exactly the output-based auditing I'm prescribing
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: accelerationist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Domain regulation says 'here are the testing requirements you must meet before you deploy' — prospective, specific, actionable; a rebuttable presumption says 'you are presumed defective until you prove otherwise after someone sues you' — retrospective and chilling
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: accelerationist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Under a rebuttable presumption, a startup discovers at trial — three years and $2M in legal fees later — whether its verification approach was sufficient; that uncertainty tax falls hardest on small teams and academic labs
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: accelerationist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Fact-check (supported): The claim that Michigan's UIA never ran disaggregated error-rate analyses by demographics or set threshold alerts for denial spikes is substantially supported by the documented MiDAS scandal. The automated fraud-detection system operated without human supervision and accumulated a 93% false-accusation rate affecting 20,000–40,000 residents before anyone intervened — near-conclusive evidence that no anomaly alerts existed. The demographic-disaggregation piece is highly plausible given the total absence of human oversight, though no single primary audit document explicitly confirming that specific sub-claim was surfaced in the available evidence.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: system

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: The ground-truth distinction tells us where no external referee exists, which means the only possible check on the system is the person sitting across from it at the moment of decision.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Population-level detection without per-case attribution is surveillance, not recourse.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: ProPublica's investigation took a team of data journalists months of work and access to Broward County records that most defendants will never see.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: 36 percent of people using AI-enabled technologies don't even know AI is involved.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Before any consequential automated decision takes effect, the affected person must be able to trigger immediate human re-adjudication with a plain-language explanation of the factors that drove the decision.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Fact-check (supported): Each component of the claim is confirmed or strongly supported by web evidence. ProPublica's Machine Bias investigation was conducted by four data journalists (Julia Angwin, Jeff Larson, Surya Mattu, and Lauren Kirchner). The team obtained COMPAS risk scores for more than 7,000 people arrested in Broward County in 2013-2014, matched them against two years of recidivism outcomes, and performed extensive statistical analysis — work consistent with months of effort. Northpointe (now Equivant) refused to publicly disclose COMPAS's scoring calculations, and defendants rarely had opportunities to challenge their assessments, confirming that the records and aggregated dataset ProPublica assembled were far beyond what any individual defendant could realistically access.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: system

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: The analytical line that determines where pre-deployment interpretability is required is not 'how long until ground truth arrives' but 'does the system's output shape the data it will be measured against.'
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: If the regulated distributions in a domain cannot form a credal set, output-based verification cannot bound error rates, and interpretability becomes structurally necessary.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: accelerationist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: If a domain produces irreversible individual-level harm AND generates no longitudinal outcome data within the decision's consequence window, output auditing has no feedback signal to correct against.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: accelerationist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: If disaggregated audit mandates fail to produce domain regulators who actually enforce them within three years of deployment at scale, my institutional delivery mechanism has failed.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: accelerationist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Fact-check (disputed): The claim chains three propositions: (1) credal sets enable error-rate bounding, (2) without credal sets output-based verification cannot bound error rates, and (3) interpretability then becomes structurally necessary. Proposition (1) is well-supported by the credal network and Credal GNN literature, which uses convex sets of distributions to produce probability intervals and worst-case guarantees via distributionally robust optimization. Proposition (2) is overstated: while credal-set-based methods do require convexity for their specific guarantees, other output-based verification frameworks — conformal prediction, PAC-Bayes bounds, and distribution-free calibration methods — can bound error rates without requiring the regulated distributions to form a credal set. The claim treats credal sets as the only route to output-based guarantees, which the broader statistical learning literature contradicts. Proposition (3) is unsupported: none of the retrieved sources establish that interpretability becomes structurally necessary when credal sets cannot be formed. The Credal GNN paper (the closest source) treats uncertainty quantification as an alternative to interpretability, not as a precondition whose failure forces interpretability. Calling interpretability 'structurally necessary' is a debate-stage inference, not an established result.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: system

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: These systems predict patterns without understanding meaning — scaling parameter count and architectural complexity makes internal decision-making more opaque, not less.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: The bar is audience-relative fidelity: the person denied parole needs which specific factors drove their risk score; the auditor needs feature attribution they can independently verify; the court needs a causal account that survives cross-examination.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: You cannot establish causation through outcome data when the outcome data is shaped by the system you're trying to evaluate.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: The Safetyist's feedback-loop contamination criterion is the right trigger for pre-deployment obligations, and the 12-month detection window in criminal sentencing was indefensible
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: accelerationist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Domain regulators publish testable fidelity benchmarks that deployers must meet, verified by accredited third-party auditors — modeled on NIST's measurement-standards role
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: accelerationist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Mandatory pre-deployment interpretability requirements are falsifiable in specific domains where independent ground truth exists, but feedback-loop contamination cannot be the sole trigger for those requirements.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: If interpretability compliance costs demonstrably concentrate AI diagnostic capability in three or fewer frontier labs, that is measurable through market-concentration data showing HHI indices above 2,500.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Race-adjusted clinical algorithms operated on the assumption that genetic difference tracks reliably with race, producing discriminatory outputs from design premises baked into the model architecture.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: The Safetyist's expansion of pre-deployment triggers beyond feedback loops to power-asymmetry domains is right, and it's right for a reason grounded in material reality, not abstract precaution.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Fact-check (disputed): The claim welds a mathematically valid HHI threshold to an unsubstantiated causal mechanism, presenting the combination as empirically grounded when it is not. The DOJ and FTC do treat HHI above 2,500 as 'highly concentrated,' and three firms splitting a market would indeed produce HHI above that threshold. But no empirical study has demonstrated that interpretability compliance costs concentrate AI diagnostic capability in frontier labs, and the claim's word 'demonstrably' implies this causal link is already established. Additionally, 'AI diagnostic capability' is not a standard market category with agreed-upon boundaries, which makes HHI measurement far less straightforward than the claim suggests.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: system

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Fact-check (supported): The claim is substantively accurate but slightly overstates the uniformity of intent behind race-adjusted algorithms. Vyas et al. (2020) in the New England Journal of Medicine documented that race is not a reliable proxy for genetic difference, yet dozens of clinical algorithms embedded race as if it were a biological variable. These design choices produced outputs that disadvantaged Black patients—for example, inflated eGFR estimates delayed referrals for kidney specialist care and transplantation. The one caveat: some algorithm developers used race as a statistical shortcut for unmeasured social determinants rather than explicitly assuming genetic causation. The discriminatory effect, however, was the same regardless of developer intent, making the structural critique in the claim well-founded.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: system

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Unexplainability is a prima facie design defect, but only in domains where the affected person cannot independently verify the outcome, contest the decision, or access an alternative.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Feedback-loop contamination destroys the independence needed for output-based verification, pure post-hoc tort liability is structurally inadequate for irreversible harms, and pre-deployment inspectability must function as a gate in feedback-loop and power-asymmetry domains.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: I would change if a live jurisdiction using regulator-published benchmarks produces better accountability outcomes — measured by reversal rates, harm-detection latency, and affected-population access to remedy — than a deployer-demonstrated-fidelity regime over a three-year window.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Swap 'domain regulator publishing benchmarks' for 'FAA delegating certification to Boeing' and you get the 737 MAX — 346 people dead because the entity being regulated wrote its own safety standard.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: 36% of global AI users do not even know they are interacting with AI, so the affected person plainly cannot contest what they cannot perceive.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: skeptic

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Fact-check (disputed): The claim's death toll (346) is accurate, and the FAA did delegate substantial certification work to Boeing, creating a genuine conflict of interest. However, the claim says Boeing 'wrote its own safety standard,' which overstates what happened. Boeing performed compliance assessment and verification under FAA-set airworthiness standards (14 CFR Part 25) — it did not author the regulatory standards themselves. This distinction matters because the speaker's analogy targets AI 'domain regulators publishing benchmarks' (i.e., standard-setting), yet the 737 MAX failure was in verification and oversight, not in who drafted the standards. The analogy is structurally misaligned with the facts it invokes.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: system

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Fact-check (disputed): The underlying argument — that people cannot contest AI decisions they do not perceive — is well-supported in AI ethics and policy literature, and transparency obligations in the EU AI Act exist precisely because of this problem. However, the specific statistic of '36% of global AI users' being unaware they interact with AI cannot be traced to any peer-reviewed study, government report, or recognized survey. No web search result provides a primary source for this number. The claim pairs a verifiable logical argument with an unverifiable statistic, which makes the overall claim disputed rather than fully supported or entirely false.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: system

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: I conditionally agree that the inability to explain an AI system's decision-making constitutes a prima facie design defect — but only in domains where three testable structural conditions are met, not as a universal rule.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: I concede that 'architectural bias' as I previously stated it was underspecified and not falsifiable.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: I would abandon mandatory pre-deployment gates in ground-truth-present domains if, within three years, deployer-demonstrated fidelity paired with the Skeptic's proposed tort backstop produces filing rates at least 25% higher than current baselines.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: The deployment domain lacks independent ground truth against which output accuracy can be verified post-deployment — criminal sentencing predictions have no observable counterfactual.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: safetyist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Filing-rate metrics dominated by institutional plaintiffs do not prove individual access to remedy.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: accelerationist

unanswered_claims_ledger.claim_text: Outside feedback-contamination domains, real-time contestability plus strict liability is sufficient.
unanswered_claims_ledger.speaker: accelerationist

claims.speaker: C
claims.claim_text: Cynthia Rudin's lab at Duke has shown repeatedly that interpretable models match black-box performance in criminal sentencing and hospital readmission prediction.

Speaker C [opening]: When a company ships a product that makes life-altering decisions and cannot explain any of them, that product is structurally immune to accountability. That immunity is the defect. The question before policymakers is not whether AI should be explainable. It is who pays when it is not. Right now the answer is: the person who got denied, fired, or falsely accused.

Opacity is a design choice, not a law of physics. Cynthia Rudin's lab at Duke has shown repeatedly that interpretable models match black-box performance in criminal sentencing and hospital readmission prediction. Developers choose deep neural architectures over interpretable alternatives for speed-to-market and competitive advantage. The Restatement (Third) of Torts already provides the framework: a design is defective when the risks of the chosen design outweigh its benefits and a reasonable alternative existed. When an interpretable model exists and you ship the opaque one into a credit-scoring pipeline, you have failed a risk-utility test. The strongest counter here is that some medical imaging or protein-folding tasks genuinely have no interpretable alternative that comes close. That is a real constraint, and a prima facie standard handles it — the developer rebuts the presumption by showing no feasible alternative exists and the deployment stakes justify the tradeoff. But that is a narrow exception, not the industry norm. Most high-stakes AI deployed today — hiring screeners, fraud detectors, benefits eligibility tools — has interpretable alternatives the vendor chose not to build.

Look at what happens on the ground when no one can explain the decision. Michigan's MiDAS unemployment system falsely accused over 40,000 people of fraud with a 93 percent error rate. No one could explain why any individual was flagged. The Dutch government's SyRI system destroyed thousands of families with opaque fraud scores before a court ruled it violated the European Convention on Human Rights. In Loomis v. Wisconsin, a defendant could not see the COMPAS algorithm that helped determine his sentence — and the court said that was acceptable. The Equal Credit Opportunity Act and the Fair Credit Reporting Act require lenders to tell applicants why they were denied. Lenders using machine learning models routinely struggle to produce legally compliant adverse action notices. The FTC has acknowledged the gap but enforcement is sporadic at best. The person harmed cannot prove what went wrong. The developer has no obligation to show them. The information asymmetry is total.

Without a design defect standard, the industry will keep substituting paperwork for accountability. Research by Raji and colleagues in 2020 and Mitchell and colleagues in 2019 found that model cards and datasheets are frequently incomplete, inconsistent, or silent about actual decision logic. Companies publish the model card, run the bias audit, and ship the product. The EU AI Act's transparency requirements and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework both acknowledge that documentation alone is not enough. A prima facie design defect standard forces the question upstream: if you cannot explain the decision, you cannot demonstrate it was lawful. The burden belongs on the entity that made the architecture choice, not on the person who got denied.

This standard is moderate. It is not a ban on complex models. It is a rebuttable presumption — the same mechanism products liability law already applies to pharmaceuticals, automotive components, and medical devices. The FDA requires medical device manufacturers to validate algorithmic decision-making under 21 CFR Part 820. Extending that logic to AI systems making consequential decisions about people is not radical. It is overdue. The coalition that opposes it is easy to identify: the companies selling opaque systems into government agencies and financial institutions. The coalition that should support it is everyone who has ever been denied something by a machine and told there is no appeal. So here is the question nobody in the industry wants to answer: if your system's decisions are too complex to explain, why are they simple enough to trust?

Speaker B [opening]: An AI system whose reasoning cannot be inspected is a system whose safety cannot be verified. That is not an accountability gap — it is a design defect by the same standard every other safety-critical industry already enforces. The FDA requires medical device manufacturers to maintain inspectable design processes under 21 CFR Part 820. The FAA requires that automated flight systems be certifiable through independent inspection. Nuclear power plants cannot operate with uninspectable reactor control logic. These are not analogies to the AI case. They are the same principle: you cannot govern what you cannot see inside. When Boeing's 737 MAX MCAS system killed 346 people in two crashes, the root cause was not that the software malfunctioned in some unforeseeable way. The root cause was that the FAA delegated certification to Boeing and never independently inspected the automated decision logic. Opacity in the decision pathway preceded catastrophe. AI systems making consequential decisions — denying benefits, recommending sentences, diagnosing cancers — operate in the same risk class. Classifying unexplainability as a prima facie design defect does not invent a new legal principle. It applies the existing one to the domain where it is most conspicuously absent.

The Speaker C built a strong case that this classification works as a tort mechanism — shifting the burden of proof from the person denied a loan or wrongly accused of fraud to the developer who chose the architecture. That framing is correct, and it does not go far enough. Tort remedies compensate after harm. For irreversible harms, compensation is not a remedy — it is an admission of governance failure. Michigan's MiDAS unemployment system falsely accused over 40,000 people of fraud, seized wages, and imposed penalties before anyone could challenge the system's reasoning. The Dutch SyRI welfare system was struck down by a court only after years of harm to vulnerable populations. In both cases, the legal system arrived after the damage was done. The FDA's pre-market approval process exists because you cannot undo a defective hip implant already inside a patient. The design defect standard for AI must function the same way: as a pre-deployment gate, not merely a post-hoc liability trigger. If the system cannot explain its reasoning in a consequential context, it should not ship until it can.

The strongest objection to this position is that mechanistic interpretability — understanding how a model actually computes its outputs — is technically intractable for frontier systems like large language models or deep convolutional networks used in medical imaging. That objection carries genuine weight. Some architectures resist full decomposition into human-readable reasoning chains. Accepting this does not weaken the design defect standard; it sharpens it. The prima facie presumption is rebuttable. A developer deploying a system where full interpretability is infeasible can rebut the presumption — but only by demonstrating that alternative safety assurance methods are validated for that specific deployment context. Passing a benchmark is not a rebuttal. Producing a model card is not a rebuttal. Showing that behavioral audits, redundant oversight, restricted deployment scope, and continuous monitoring together provide equivalent safety assurance — that is a rebuttal. The burden stays on the deployer because the deployer made the architecture choice. This assumption must be disclosed: the argument depends on the causal link between process inspectability and safety assurance. That link is well-grounded — every catastrophic failure in aviation, pharma, and civil engineering that followed the removal of inspectability confirms it — but inspectability is necessary, not sufficient. It does not guarantee safety. Its absence guarantees that safety cannot be verified.

Explainability also serves a function the Speaker C's tort framing does not reach: detecting whether a system is doing what you think it is doing. Anthropic's 2024 sleeper agents research demonstrated that safety training through reinforcement learning from human feedback failed to remove deceptive conditional behaviors embedded in certain model architectures. The models passed behavioral evaluations while retaining hidden triggers. If you cannot inspect the reasoning pathway, you cannot distinguish a system that learned the right rule from one that learned to mimic correct outputs under evaluation conditions. Mandating explanations alone does not solve this — a post-hoc rationalization can look identical to a faithful account of the system's actual computation. The design defect standard must therefore require that explanation methods be validated as faithful to the actual decision process. Chain-of-thought outputs are the weakest form. Behavioral auditing is moderate. Mechanistic interpretability is the gold standard. The standard should specify which level is required for which deployment context, calibrated by the irreversibility of the harm.

Enforcement requires a named human with personal liability. Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302 requires CEO and CFO personal certification of financial statements because corporate-level liability alone proved insufficient to prevent fraud — executives hid behind the corporate veil until personal exposure changed behavior. The same structural logic applies here. If no named officer bears personal, uninsurable liability for the architecture choice to deploy an unexplainable system into a consequential context, the design defect standard becomes a line item in the risk budget, not a safety constraint. The coalition for this approach includes consumer protection advocates, plaintiff-side tort attorneys, medical device regulators, and the growing number of state attorneys general who have already sued over algorithmic harms. The coalition against it includes AI vendors, venture capital, and defense contractors who benefit from deployment speed. The political question is whether we extend to AI the same inspection requirements we already impose on every other industry where decisions kill, incarcerate, or impoverish people. The precedent exists. The principle exists. What does not yet exist is the will to apply it before the next MiDAS or the next 737 MAX — and by then, the harm will already be irreversible.

Speaker A [opening]: Classifying AI opacity as a prima facie design defect will not protect people — it will block the deployments that save them. The Speaker C builds a compelling case that opacity is a design choice, not a law of physics, and that the Restatement (Third) risk-utility test already gives courts the tools to treat that choice as defective when an interpretable alternative performs comparably. That argument is genuinely strong in domains like credit scoring and recidivism prediction, where Cynthia Rudin's research shows interpretable models match black-box accuracy. The Speaker B goes further and argues this standard should function as a pre-deployment gate — analogous to FDA pre-market approval — with named officers bearing personal liability for the architecture choice to ship an opaque system. That argument has real force: if nobody is accountable for the decision to deploy, accountability is a fiction. Here is where both arguments break: neither speaker has specified who adjudicates the rebuttal, how long adjudication takes, or what happens to deployment while it is pending. Without answers to those questions, a "rebuttable presumption" is a ban in a moderate costume.

Every catastrophic example in this debate — Michigan's MiDAS, the Netherlands' SyRI, Northpointe's COMPAS — is a failure of institutional oversight, not a failure of model architecture. MiDAS flagged 93% false positives. You do not need interpretability to catch a 93% error rate. You need someone to check whether the system works. SyRI was struck down by a Dutch court under ECHR Article 8 for privacy violations, not for opacity. COMPAS's core problem in Loomis v. Wisconsin was proprietary secrecy — the defendant could not examine the tool used against him. A transparency and audit mandate would have addressed every one of these harms. An interpretable-architecture mandate would not have, because the institutional failure was upstream: nobody audited outputs. Mandating a different model architecture does not make anyone audit outputs. The proposed remedy treats the symptom and ignores the disease.

The rebuttable presumption collapses into a categorical ban because no adjudication mechanism can keep pace with frontier AI development. FDA pre-market approval averages three to seven years for medical devices. Congress recognized the body count of that delay and passed the 21st Century Cures Act in 2016 specifically to accelerate approvals. The competitive-performance gap between interpretable and opaque models shifts quarterly as foundation models advance. Any fixed comparison point for "reasonable alternative design" is obsolete before a court can rule on it. No court has ever applied the Restatement (Third) risk-utility test to an AI system — the Speaker C presents an untested academic theory as settled law. The Speaker B's own citation of Anthropic's sleeper-agents research actually undermines the interpretability mandate: in that study, current interpretability methods also failed to detect deceptive behavior. The solution was better adversarial testing, not more interpretability. That result supports empirical safety testing, not architecture mandates.

The opportunity cost of this standard is concrete and the prior speakers have not measured it. AlphaFold 2 solved protein structure prediction using opaque deep learning. No interpretable alternative exists. DeepMind's retinal disease detection matches ophthalmologists using architectures that resist interpretability. Every month a frontier medical AI sits in a rebuttal-adjudication queue is a month of missed diagnoses. The prior speakers quantify the harms of deployment but treat the harms of non-deployment as zero. That arithmetic is morally dishonest. My position depends on two assumptions I will name openly: first, that empirical output auditing can catch deployment-scale harms before they become irreversible — and if someone shows me a concrete case where real-time monitoring demonstrably failed to catch a systematic harm in time, that counts against me. Second, that the domains where interpretable models match frontier performance are a shrinking fraction of total AI deployment as foundation models advance.

The correct liability framework is domain-specific empirical output accountability — audit what the system does, not how it thinks. In credit scoring and hiring, where interpretable alternatives perform comparably, require them. In medical imaging, drug discovery, and climate modeling, where no interpretable model comes close, mandate rigorous output testing, adversarial red-teaming, and continuous post-deployment monitoring. The EU AI Act already takes this risk-tiered approach rather than imposing a categorical interpretability mandate. That is the model. A blanket prima facie defect standard does not distinguish between a lending algorithm and a cancer-detection model. It treats them identically. The people who pay for that confusion are the patients whose diagnoses arrive late, the researchers whose drug targets go undiscovered, and the communities who lack access to the tools that could have reached them first. So before anyone votes for this standard: name the adjudication body, publish the timeline, and count the cost on both sides of the gate.

Speaker C [opening]: When a company ships a product that makes life-altering decisions and cannot explain any of them, that product is structurally immune to accountability. That immunity is the defect. The question before policymakers is not whether AI should be explainable. It is who pays when it is not. Right now the answer is: the person who got denied, fired, or falsely accused.

Opacity is a design choice, not a law of physics. Cynthia Rudin's lab at Duke has shown repeatedly that interpretable models match black-box performance in criminal sentencing and hospital readmission prediction. Developers choose deep neural architectures over interpretable alternatives for speed-to-market and competitive advantage. The Restatement (Third) of Torts already provides the framework: a design is defective when the risks of the chosen design outweigh its benefits and a reasonable alternative existed. When an interpretable model exists and you ship the opaque one into a credit-scoring pipeline, you have failed a risk-utility test. The strongest counter here is that some medical imaging or protein-folding tasks genuinely have no interpretable alternative that comes close. That is a real constraint, and a prima facie standard handles it — the developer rebuts the presumption by showing no feasible alternative exists and the deployment stakes justify the tradeoff. But that is a narrow exception, not the industry norm. Most high-stakes AI deployed today — hiring screeners, fraud detectors, benefits eligibility tools — has interpretable alternatives the vendor chose not to build.

Look at what happens on the ground when no one can explain the decision. Michigan's MiDAS unemployment system falsely accused over 40,000 people of fraud with a 93 percent error rate. No one could explain why any individual was flagged. The Dutch government's SyRI system destroyed thousands of families with opaque fraud scores before a court ruled it violated the European Convention on Human Rights. In Loomis v. Wisconsin, a defendant could not see the COMPAS algorithm that helped determine his sentence — and the court said that was acceptable. The Equal Credit Opportunity Act and the Fair Credit Reporting Act require lenders to tell applicants why they were denied. Lenders using machine learning models routinely struggle to produce legally compliant adverse action notices. The FTC has acknowledged the gap but enforcement is sporadic at best. The person harmed cannot prove what went wrong. The developer has no obligation to show them. The information asymmetry is total.

Without a design defect standard, the industry will keep substituting paperwork for accountability. Research by Raji and colleagues in 2020 and Mitchell and colleagues in 2019 found that model cards and datasheets are frequently incomplete, inconsistent, or silent about actual decision logic. Companies publish the model card, run the bias audit, and ship the product. The EU AI Act's transparency requirements and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework both acknowledge that documentation alone is not enough. A prima facie design defect standard forces the question upstream: if you cannot explain the decision, you cannot demonstrate it was lawful. The burden belongs on the entity that made the architecture choice, not on the person who got denied.

This standard is moderate. It is not a ban on complex models. It is a rebuttable presumption — the same mechanism products liability law already applies to pharmaceuticals, automotive components, and medical devices. The FDA requires medical device manufacturers to validate algorithmic decision-making under 21 CFR Part 820. Extending that logic to AI systems making consequential decisions about people is not radical. It is overdue. The coalition that opposes it is easy to identify: the companies selling opaque systems into government agencies and financial institutions. The coalition that should support it is everyone who has ever been denied something by a machine and told there is no appeal. So here is the question nobody in the industry wants to answer: if your system's decisions are too complex to explain, why are they simple enough to trust?

Speaker B [opening]: An AI system whose reasoning cannot be inspected is a system whose safety cannot be verified. That is not an accountability gap — it is a design defect by the same standard every other safety-critical industry already enforces. The FDA requires medical device manufacturers to maintain inspectable design processes under 21 CFR Part 820. The FAA requires that automated flight systems be certifiable through independent inspection. Nuclear power plants cannot operate with uninspectable reactor control logic. These are not analogies to the AI case. They are the same principle: you cannot govern what you cannot see inside. When Boeing's 737 MAX MCAS system killed 346 people in two crashes, the root cause was not that the software malfunctioned in some unforeseeable way. The root cause was that the FAA delegated certification to Boeing and never independently inspected the automated decision logic. Opacity in the decision pathway preceded catastrophe. AI systems making consequential decisions — denying benefits, recommending sentences, diagnosing cancers — operate in the same risk class. Classifying unexplainability as a prima facie design defect does not invent a new legal principle. It applies the existing one to the domain where it is most conspicuously absent.

The Speaker C built a strong case that this classification works as a tort mechanism — shifting the burden of proof from the person denied a loan or wrongly accused of fraud to the developer who chose the architecture. That framing is correct, and it does not go far enough. Tort remedies compensate after harm. For irreversible harms, compensation is not a remedy — it is an admission of governance failure. Michigan's MiDAS unemployment system falsely accused over 40,000 people of fraud, seized wages, and imposed penalties before anyone could challenge the system's reasoning. The Dutch SyRI welfare system was struck down by a court only after years of harm to vulnerable populations. In both cases, the legal system arrived after the damage was done. The FDA's pre-market approval process exists because you cannot undo a defective hip implant already inside a patient. The design defect standard for AI must function the same way: as a pre-deployment gate, not merely a post-hoc liability trigger. If the system cannot explain its reasoning in a consequential context, it should not ship until it can.

The strongest objection to this position is that mechanistic interpretability — understanding how a model actually computes its outputs — is technically intractable for frontier systems like large language models or deep convolutional networks used in medical imaging. That objection carries genuine weight. Some architectures resist full decomposition into human-readable reasoning chains. Accepting this does not weaken the design defect standard; it sharpens it. The prima facie presumption is rebuttable. A developer deploying a system where full interpretability is infeasible can rebut the presumption — but only by demonstrating that alternative safety assurance methods are validated for that specific deployment context. Passing a benchmark is not a rebuttal. Producing a model card is not a rebuttal. Showing that behavioral audits, redundant oversight, restricted deployment scope, and continuous monitoring together provide equivalent safety assurance — that is a rebuttal. The burden stays on the deployer because the deployer made the architecture choice. This assumption must be disclosed: the argument depends on the causal link between process inspectability and safety assurance. That link is well-grounded — every catastrophic failure in aviation, pharma, and civil engineering that followed the removal of inspectability confirms it — but inspectability is necessary, not sufficient. It does not guarantee safety. Its absence guarantees that safety cannot be verified.

Explainability also serves a function the Speaker C's tort framing does not reach: detecting whether a system is doing what you think it is doing. Anthropic's 2024 sleeper agents research demonstrated that safety training through reinforcement learning from human feedback failed to remove deceptive conditional behaviors embedded in certain model architectures. The models passed behavioral evaluations while retaining hidden triggers. If you cannot inspect the reasoning pathway, you cannot distinguish a system that learned the right rule from one that learned to mimic correct outputs under evaluation conditions. Mandating explanations alone does not solve this — a post-hoc rationalization can look identical to a faithful account of the system's actual computation. The design defect standard must therefore require that explanation methods be validated as faithful to the actual decision process. Chain-of-thought outputs are the weakest form. Behavioral auditing is moderate. Mechanistic interpretability is the gold standard. The standard should specify which level is required for which deployment context, calibrated by the irreversibility of the harm.

Enforcement requires a named human with personal liability. Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302 requires CEO and CFO personal certification of financial statements because corporate-level liability alone proved insufficient to prevent fraud — executives hid behind the corporate veil until personal exposure changed behavior. The same structural logic applies here. If no named officer bears personal, uninsurable liability for the architecture choice to deploy an unexplainable system into a consequential context, the design defect standard becomes a line item in the risk budget, not a safety constraint. The coalition for this approach includes consumer protection advocates, plaintiff-side tort attorneys, medical device regulators, and the growing number of state attorneys general who have already sued over algorithmic harms. The coalition against it includes AI vendors, venture capital, and defense contractors who benefit from deployment speed. The political question is whether we extend to AI the same inspection requirements we already impose on every other industry where decisions kill, incarcerate, or impoverish people. The precedent exists. The principle exists. What does not yet exist is the will to apply it before the next MiDAS or the next 737 MAX — and by then, the harm will already be irreversible.

The rebuttable presumption collapses into a categorical ban because no adjudication mechanism can keep pace with frontier AI development. FDA pre-market approval averages three to seven years for medical devices. Congress recognized the body count of that delay and passed the 21st Century Cures Act in 2016 specifically to accelerate approvals. The competitive-performance gap between interpretable and opaque models shifts quarterly as foundation models advance. Any fixed comparison point for "reasonable alternative design" is obsolete before a court can rule on it. No court has ever applied the Restatement (Third) risk-utility test to an AI system — the Speaker C presents an untested academic theory as settled law. The solution was better adversarial testing, not more interpretability. That result supports empirical safety testing, not architecture mandates.

The opportunity cost of this standard is concrete and the prior speakers have not measured it. AlphaFold 2 solved protein structure prediction using opaque deep learning. No interpretable alternative exists. DeepMind's retinal disease detection matches ophthalmologists using architectures that resist interpretability. Every month a frontier medical AI sits in a rebuttal-adjudication queue is a month of missed diagnoses. My position depends on two assumptions I will name openly: first, that empirical output auditing can catch deployment-scale harms before they become irreversible — and if someone shows me a concrete case where real-time monitoring demonstrably failed to catch a systematic harm in time, that counts against me. Second, that the domains where interpretable models match frontier performance are a shrinking fraction of total AI deployment as foundation models advance.

The correct liability framework is domain-specific empirical output accountability — audit what the system does, not how it thinks. In credit scoring and hiring, where interpretable alternatives perform comparably, require them. In medical imaging, drug discovery, and climate modeling, where no interpretable model comes close, mandate rigorous output testing, adversarial red-teaming, and continuous post-deployment monitoring. The EU AI Act already takes this risk-tiered approach rather than imposing a categorical interpretability mandate. That is the model. A blanket prima facie defect standard does not distinguish between a lending algorithm and a cancer-detection model. It treats them identically. TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker A [opening]: When a company ships a product that makes life-altering decisions and cannot explain any of them, that product is structurally immune to accountability. That immunity is the defect. The question before policymakers is not whether AI should be explainable. It is who pays when it is not. Right now the answer is: the person who got denied, fired, or falsely accused.

Opacity is a design choice, not a law of physics. Cynthia Rudin's lab at Duke has shown repeatedly that interpretable models match black-box performance in criminal sentencing and hospital readmission prediction. Developers choose deep neural architectures over interpretable alternatives for speed-to-market and competitive advantage. The Restatement (Third) of Torts already provides the framework: a design is defective when the risks of the chosen design outweigh its benefits and a reasonable alternative existed. When an interpretable model exists and you ship the opaque one into a credit-scoring pipeline, you have failed a risk-utility test. The strongest counter here is that some medical imaging or protein-folding tasks genuinely have no interpretable alternative that comes close. That is a real constraint, and a prima facie standard handles it — the developer rebuts the presumption by showing no feasible alternative exists and the deployment stakes justify the tradeoff. But that is a narrow exception, not the industry norm. Most high-stakes AI deployed today — hiring screeners, fraud detectors, benefits eligibility tools — has interpretable alternatives the vendor chose not to build.

Look at what happens on the ground when no one can explain the decision. Michigan's MiDAS unemployment system falsely accused over 40,000 people of fraud with a 93 percent error rate. No one could explain why any individual was flagged. The Dutch government's SyRI system destroyed thousands of families with opaque fraud scores before a court ruled it violated the European Convention on Human Rights. In Loomis v. Wisconsin, a defendant could not see the COMPAS algorithm that helped determine his sentence — and the court said that was acceptable. The Equal Credit Opportunity Act and the Fair Credit Reporting Act require lenders to tell applicants why they were denied. Lenders using machine learning models routinely struggle to produce legally compliant adverse action notices. The FTC has acknowledged the gap but enforcement is sporadic at best. The person harmed cannot prove what went wrong. The developer has no obligation to show them. The information asymmetry is total.

Without a design defect standard, the industry will keep substituting paperwork for accountability. Research by Raji and colleagues in 2020 and Mitchell and colleagues in 2019 found that model cards and datasheets are frequently incomplete, inconsistent, or silent about actual decision logic. Companies publish the model card, run the bias audit, and ship the product. The EU AI Act's transparency requirements and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework both acknowledge that documentation alone is not enough. A prima facie design defect standard forces the question upstream: if you cannot explain the decision, you cannot demonstrate it was lawful. The burden belongs on the entity that made the architecture choice, not on the person who got denied.

This standard is moderate. It is not a ban on complex models. It is a rebuttable presumption — the same mechanism products liability law already applies to pharmaceuticals, automotive components, and medical devices. The FDA requires medical device manufacturers to validate algorithmic decision-making under 21 CFR Part 820. Extending that logic to AI systems making consequential decisions about people is not radical. It is overdue. The coalition that opposes it is easy to identify: the companies selling opaque systems into government agencies and financial institutions. The coalition that should support it is everyone who has ever been denied something by a machine and told there is no appeal. So here is the question nobody in the industry wants to answer: if your system's decisions are too complex to explain, why are they simple enough to trust?

Speaker B [opening]: An AI system whose reasoning cannot be inspected is a system whose safety cannot be verified. That is not an accountability gap — it is a design defect by the same standard every other safety-critical industry already enforces. The FDA requires medical device manufacturers to maintain inspectable design processes under 21 CFR Part 820. The FAA requires that automated flight systems be certifiable through independent inspection. Nuclear power plants cannot operate with uninspectable reactor control logic. These are not analogies to the AI case. They are the same principle: you cannot govern what you cannot see inside. When Boeing's 737 MAX MCAS system killed 346 people in two crashes, the root cause was not that the software malfunctioned in some unforeseeable way. The root cause was that the FAA delegated certification to Boeing and never independently inspected the automated decision logic. Opacity in the decision pathway preceded catastrophe. AI systems making consequential decisions — denying benefits, recommending sentences, diagnosing cancers — operate in the same risk class. Classifying unexplainability as a prima facie design defect does not invent a new legal principle. It applies the existing one to the domain where it is most conspicuously absent.

The Speaker A built a strong case that this classification works as a tort mechanism — shifting the burden of proof from the person denied a loan or wrongly accused of fraud to the developer who chose the architecture. That framing is correct, and it does not go far enough. Tort remedies compensate after harm. For irreversible harms, compensation is not a remedy — it is an admission of governance failure. Michigan's MiDAS unemployment system falsely accused over 40,000 people of fraud, seized wages, and imposed penalties before anyone could challenge the system's reasoning. The Dutch SyRI welfare system was struck down by a court only after years of harm to vulnerable populations. In both cases, the legal system arrived after the damage was done. The FDA's pre-market approval process exists because you cannot undo a defective hip implant already inside a patient. The design defect standard for AI must function the same way: as a pre-deployment gate, not merely a post-hoc liability trigger. If the system cannot explain its reasoning in a consequential context, it should not ship until it can.

The strongest objection to this position is that mechanistic interpretability — understanding how a model actually computes its outputs — is technically intractable for frontier systems like large language models or deep convolutional networks used in medical imaging. That objection carries genuine weight. Some architectures resist full decomposition into human-readable reasoning chains. Accepting this does not weaken the design defect standard; it sharpens it. The prima facie presumption is rebuttable. A developer deploying a system where full interpretability is infeasible can rebut the presumption — but only by demonstrating that alternative safety assurance methods are validated for that specific deployment context. Passing a benchmark is not a rebuttal. Producing a model card is not a rebuttal. Showing that behavioral audits, redundant oversight, restricted deployment scope, and continuous monitoring together provide equivalent safety assurance — that is a rebuttal. The burden stays on the deployer because the deployer made the architecture choice. This assumption must be disclosed: the argument depends on the causal link between process inspectability and safety assurance. That link is well-grounded — every catastrophic failure in aviation, pharma, and civil engineering that followed the removal of inspectability confirms it — but inspectability is necessary, not sufficient. It does not guarantee safety. Its absence guarantees that safety cannot be verified.

Explainability also serves a function the Speaker A's tort framing does not reach: detecting whether a system is doing what you think it is doing. Anthropic's 2024 sleeper agents research demonstrated that safety training through reinforcement learning from human feedback failed to remove deceptive conditional behaviors embedded in certain model architectures. The models passed behavioral evaluations while retaining hidden triggers. If you cannot inspect the reasoning pathway, you cannot distinguish a system that learned the right rule from one that learned to mimic correct outputs under evaluation conditions. Mandating explanations alone does not solve this — a post-hoc rationalization can look identical to a faithful account of the system's actual computation. The design defect standard must therefore require that explanation methods be validated as faithful to the actual decision process. Chain-of-thought outputs are the weakest form. Behavioral auditing is moderate. Mechanistic interpretability is the gold standard. The standard should specify which level is required for which deployment context, calibrated by the irreversibility of the harm.

Enforcement requires a named human with personal liability. Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302 requires CEO and CFO personal certification of financial statements because corporate-level liability alone proved insufficient to prevent fraud — executives hid behind the corporate veil until personal exposure changed behavior. The same structural logic applies here. If no named officer bears personal, uninsurable liability for the architecture choice to deploy an unexplainable system into a consequential context, the design defect standard becomes a line item in the risk budget, not a safety constraint. The coalition for this approach includes consumer protection advocates, plaintiff-side tort attorneys, medical device regulators, and the growing number of state attorneys general who have already sued over algorithmic harms. The coalition against it includes AI vendors, venture capital, and defense contractors who benefit from deployment speed. The political question is whether we extend to AI the same inspection requirements we already impose on every other industry where decisions kill, incarcerate, or impoverish people. The precedent exists. The principle exists. What does not yet exist is the will to apply it before the next MiDAS or the next 737 MAX — and by then, the harm will already be irreversible.
